items.body: Is Woven Ground an EP with an accompanying film, or a film with an accompanying EP? We’ll leave it to the project’s viewers and listeners and to decide. Either way, Blair Coron‘s multi-media release is a treat for the eyes and ears, a celebration of Scottish forests, islands and glens, filled with lush instrumentation, poetry and harmony, coupled with sumptuous landscapes and insightful interviews. As Coron explains, “I could never say, ‘This song is the river’ or ‘these words are the forest’ … so I took my instruments and recording equipment and friends to the places I was writing about.” The landscapes are first seen from a moving car, then the disembarking, revealing the sounds of the village and the port. In the early minutes, Coron celebrates the gift of the Isle of Canna, a sacred trust and sanctuary. The cows seem as relaxed as the strings and historical piano, or the other way around. The views are bucolic, the pace of life unhurried, the area seemingly free from pollution, time in suspension. The natural soundscape is allowed to take center stage (more detectable in the film than the EP). In the first interview, one learns of apple trees fertilized by the bodies of seals. Farmland equipment lies abandoned; an ancient church stands witness. Local residents express pride in their location and history. Shoes off, windows open, Coron engages with the piano; “Isle of Canna, Midsummer, 5:54am, 2026” arrives a third of the way into the film, but is the EP’s opening piece, a love letter to the location. The next piece takes a little more work; a harmonium is not an easy instrument to move, especially across uneven terrain. The sprightly “Sgùrr A’ Mhaoraich” is performed by a babbling brook, with Charlie Stewart on the much more portable fiddle. The piece is an ode to the countryside and the flowing water, whose music never ends. As the camera zooms in to the reel-to-reel, the recording device begins to look like a stream. Coron sits outdoors at a table, reciting “Beneath Six Black Poplar Trees,” a poem that looks back to the dawn of creation, with creation itself the accompaniment. His voice is comforting, with gentle inflection that matches the spider webs undulating in the wind. The strings return, setting up the gorgeous closer, which includes Miwa Nagato-Apthorp and Zoe Bestel on layered vocals. “Hymn,” while not on the EP, is one of the highlights of the film (35:12-38:06, a music video on its own). An adjacent version was released on the Two Old Songs EP in April, the original on On the Nature of Things, but we like this choral version the best. For “Moon Lament,” the quartet sits in the woods, captivated and captivating, having become part of the visual and sonic scenery, melting into the forest like the voices of the water and the wind. This ebullient song is chased by warm laughter and the twittering of birds; the camera draws back, revealing canopies of green. Woven Ground the EP becomes a souvenir of Woven Ground the film. The images resurface when playing the music, stored in the memory as the seeds are stored in the earth. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by Cicero 3.14 — Among the recent live albums I've had the chance to review, some were accompanied by choreographedperformances that are hard to appreciate when you only have the audio. Yet, combining dance withprog for a unique evening seems to be a growing trend. This was the case for the wonderful livealbum by Ana�d, as well as Le Orme's *La Gondola*. So, where does this live album by Runaway Totem?aband with such a unique approach?fit in?Founded by Roberto Gottardi in 1988, RT has 14 albums to its name, including two live releases. Thisis the third?a double album. Initially classified as Zeuhl, RT was already transcending the genrewhen I saw them in 2015. At the time, the vocalist was Raffaello Regoli (frontman of Cormorano, whomI reviewed recently), and I was somewhat disappointed when I met the band the day after the concertand they asked for my opinion. In fact, I believe that having multiple creative forces involvedrequires a catalyst that is difficult to achieve. Roberto is now solely at the helm; this albumoffers greater coherence in showcasing the project's ambitions, and Andromaca?an experimentalItalian duo featuring Antonella Suella (vocals) and Stefano Bertoli (keyboards, programming,Ableton)?proves to be an excellent partner here. CD1 is titled *Searching for a New Dimension*; inhis brief stage introduction, Roberto mentions Krautrock, and that is indeed where one should lookfor points of reference. Electronic and psychedelic sounds, infused with Indian percussion andfeaturing distinct, unexpected nods?such as Pink Floyd's "On the Run" or Tangerine Dream's"Stratosfear"?blend naturally into this continuous 45-minute sequence. The final section, with itsguttural incantations, brings this first journey to a powerful and deeply soulful close. CD2, *Onthe Edge of Space and Time*, offers a series of tracks interspersed with Roberto's spokenintroductions; it includes "Heliocentric Energy," an enlightening vocal-versus-synth duel?a far cryfrom the Page/Plant dynamic! I'll wrap up there, as "enlightening" is exactly how I felt afterlistening to this album. Two hours spent in another world...Originaly published in french on Prog censor's FB pages

items.body: Review by alainPP — This EP marks a period of reflection following the departure of two band members, including Charlie. So, is it a transition or an evolution?"In a Fever Dream" is a gentle, melancholic acoustic track with whispered vocals, a fragile sound that develops into atmospheric djent metal with thunderous riffs and trip-hop influences. The lyrics explore a sense of disorientation?a sign of things to come? The contrast with the drum polyrhythms and savage growls, the restrained, solemn crescendo, and the surprising Ross, is striking. "Delirium" features a piercing, syncopated riff over an industrial beat and a Haken-esque chorus. The djent element returns on this tightly packed, flawless track, culminating in an explosive, exhilarating outro that launches into "Eclipsed by You," a slow-tempo track that veers between staccato metallic vocals, a deafening groove, and progressive keyboard electronics. The track is linear and highly professional, a testament to the innovative nature of this song, which balances unbridled gentleness with restrained violence."Bleeding Sky" boasts a subtle, syncopated groove and the ever-present vocals, a hallmark of this band. An ambient break reminds us that HAKEN has a distinctly modern prog-djent metal signature with its hypnotic crescendo. The crackling pads give way to cinematic, bucolic bird sounds. "Lotus," with its ethereal piano, offers a gentle opening; a captivating, hypnotic sound with an oppressive groove. The djent guitar enters over Ross's distant, trembling growl. The alternation between the break and the long, atmospheric drift sounds like a fresco faded by time, lacking in ferocity, and Ross's falsetto reinforces this ethereal, post-rock feel.HAKEN returns to visceral, more technical prog-metal. A deceptively complex album, far more intricate than it initially appears.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'One Among the Living' is the fourth studio album released by Canadian band Mystery, and to this dayit remains one of their most appreciated and recognizable works. A complex conceptual record, thiselegantly arranged LP offers a melodically-inclined style of neo-progressive rock that is informedboth by the genre's progenitors, and by the glamorous sounds of the 80s AOR/pop rock scene in theUK. Fans of contemporary neo-prog shall recognize many of the traits shared by bands like Pendragon,Galahad, and Arena, in the melodic guitars, opulent keyboard textures, and that fine blend betweensymphonic music and traditional rock instrumentation.The arrangements are intricate and the soundscapes are lush, while the overall atmosphere of 'One Among the Living' seems to be brooding, epic, and even theatrical. And while there certainly are strong ideas with solid execution, 'OneAmong the Living' often feels like something you have already heard, offering familiar sounds thatperfectly fit the neo-prog landscape of the late 2000s. I lack a bit of edge and novelty with thisalbum, even if the emotionally-loaded performances of singer Benoît David are tremendous and praise-worthy. The songs 'Wolf', 'The Falling Man' and the title track might be the strongest entries here,whereas most instrumental sections in 'Till the Truth Comes Out' and 'Through Different Eyes' arequite excellent, too. The rest is way too mellow for my taste, but enjoyers of the neo-prog subgenrewill definitely have plenty of gorgeous material to explore on this 2010 Unicorn Digital release.

items.body: Review by Second Life Syndrome — Originally written for theprogmind.comThe Emerald Dawn are back with Volume II of their epic, The Land, the Sea, the Air. The band has produced consistently, with increasing quality, over the past decade, and that continues here. This might be my favorite album from them (maybe second favorite after To Touch the Sky). Regardless, more people need to give them a shot.The Emerald Dawn comes to us from St. Ives, UK. They are four-strong, having the same lineup for the last seven years or so. The players are Ally Carter on guitars, soprano and tenor saxophones, and keyboards; Tree Stewart on vocals, keyboards, flute, handSonic, and Roli Seaboard; Dave Greenaway on 6-string bass, and Tom Jackson on drums.They play progressive rock that avoids the cliches. The songs are atmospheric and organic, not to mention quite lengthy. They sound like they could be straight out of the 70s, yet their sound is ever fresh to me simply because they don't really sound like anyone else. Their music is ethereal, mystical, spacious, and even a bit like a folk ritual at times.By now, everything about their sound is like comfort food for my soul: Ally's growling guitars, Tree's illustrious keys and flute, Dave's energetic bass, and Tom intricate drumming. There's a reason why all four of them end up in my top musician features every time they release an album: they are amazingly skilled players who value expression over technicality, authenticity over plasticity. And for my money? Tree has probably laid down the best keyboard performance of the year, swooning and flowing with clarity and majesty. All of the performances are incredible, though.The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) follows the first volume from 2025, which I rather liked. But I think this one is stronger. It has only three songs, in true Emerald Dawn fashion. The first one is called 'Song of the Rainforest', which is twenty-one minutes long. And yet, it is one of my favorite songs by the band to this point. This lengthy instrumental piece is so atmospheric, but somehow also so groovy. The song pulls you into its foliage, and underneath those trees is plenty of searing synth, amazing sax segments, gorgeous melodies, and hypnotic portions that feel otherworldly. I particularly love the precious minutes towards the end that hover with smoky flute, like a spellbinding incense rich with emotion.The second track is 'Rivers of Tears', which is fifteen minutes long. This one took a little more time for me, but I've come to love the focus on piano. It has a bluesy, funk-oriented sound at times, and much of it is reserved and building towards something. The song is structured with more energetic portions in the middle and the end, and each half has its own character, one being piano expressions and the other being more sinister. It's a brilliant track.The final track is called 'Paradise', being about nine minutes long. And you know what? It's yet another favorite from the band. I can't get enough of it right now, actually. It's the most 'normal' song on the album, featuring great vocals from Tree, who also plays her cosmic heart out on the keys. Seriously, this track is both incredibly groovy, almost making me what to dance (almost), but the layers of keyboard melodies, the catchiness of the hook, and the final minutes of sheer instrumental glory are like celestial medicine for the mind. What a finish!The Emerald Dawn are seasoned musicians, yes, but they are passionate artists who truly feel the flow, taste the melody, visualize the color, hear the beating heart of it all. The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) has some of their best work, both calming and foreboding at times. It is a balanced, well-written record that makes you want to start it over again as soon as it ends.

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — Scotland's most famous band returns in the early fourth quarter of 2026 with its ninth studio album, "A Song for Tomorrow." It is a soundtrack that traverses the Bible, politics, technology, and the (all-too) many conflicts around the globe to explore what lies behind sensationalist media headlines?namely people, their relationships, their emotions, and their experiences."A Song for Tomorrow" presents the dichotomy between our inner selves and the image we project to the world around us: our dreams, the reasons we get up every morning, our falls and recoveries?everything that ultimately defines the human being.PALLAS has chosen a range of themes encompassing environmental collapse, digital surveillance, fracturing relationships, and the unsettling noises of our daily lives. It is a record that showcases the voices of all four band members on equal footing, with each contributing both lead and backing vocals. Did you like the artwork for "The Messenger"? Rest assured, this one is even better; the liner notes reveal nothing about the current hot topic?AI. Mike Bentley is considered the fifth member of PALLAS.The album opens strongly with "Reset" (9/10)?the shortest track on the record, yet one of true beauty that flows effortlessly. It segues into "Rage," a more muscular, almost metallic, and slightly longer track?a piece where Niall Mathewson proves, if proof were needed, that he is a master guitarist (9/10), delivering a sound reminiscent of a wild, Rush-esque soundtrack. "A Song for Tomorrow"?the title track?features the childlike vocals of Natasha O'Neal (who also collaborates with Niall on other musical projects); it is a very calm track until the 4:34 mark, when it intensifies somewhat in the finale, driven by layered backing vocals (9/10). Next up is the epic "The Private Collector," clocking in at over eight minutes; it places Pallas back at the heart of the symphonic progressive rock style the Scottish quartet has mastered since its early days (revisit "The Sentinel" or "The Wedge"?this track is very close to that sound, perhaps leaning more towards the latter). It is a timeless gem?nothing more needs to be said (10/10).The next two tracks, "Dirt" and "Aspirations," are of similar length and tempo; it is hard to say which I prefer. "Dirt" is more accessible and commercial (reminiscent of certain tracks on *The Cross and the Crucible*), whereas "Aspirations" is gentler, featuring quasi-religious backing vocals and Graeme Murray's twelve-string guitar taking center stage (9/10 for the former, 8/10 for the latter). "Rushing Headlong" is far more frenetic?another short piece, and thankfully so, as it was the only track on the album I genuinely disliked; it is chaotic?a term I sometimes use?and messy (6/10).The final three tracks?comprising a third of the album's total runtime?represent the very best of the symphonic progressive rock genre, of which Pallas has long been a leading light. First is "The Avenue of Broken Dreams," featuring a slow rhythmic build-up, Ronnie Brown's atmospheric keyboards, and Niall Matthewson's guitar work?lyrical, inventive, and tastefully restrained. A musical delight (9/10). Then, the shorter, calmer "Mother" (8/10) serves as a breather before what follows: the concluding track, "Inside Outside." This piece distills the very essence of what has defined PALLAS for decades into just over nine minutes. It is a melodic ascent showcasing the musicians at their peak, featuring the kind of soaring lead vocals and magnificent backing harmonies we love, alongside top-tier symphonic elements (10/10).As a side note, the absence of a real drummer didn't bother me in the slightest; Niall and Ronnie split the percussion programming duties depending on the track. It will be interesting to see how this translates to the stage during the band's final tour in a few weeks, as Alan Reed's illness is forcing the Scottish group to cease live performances.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Shifting from the brutal to the delicate within a single song - one of the hallmarks that Opeth handled with ease - reached a turning point with the groundbreaking "Damnation" (2003), an album that almost entirely dispenses with the hostile sounds of extreme metal to embrace the most melodic aspects of '70s progressive rock. A risky decision that, despite initial concerns, demonstrated the band's versatility in moving confidently between different musical styles, while leaving fans and critics alike wondering about the direction the band would take in the future.With "Ghost Reveries" (2005), their eighth album, the Swedes once again use death metal as one of the fundamental elements of their sound, integrated with progressive components that are far more developed than in their previous works. Mikael �kerfeldt's demonic growls, the monolithic and dense guitar riffs of Peter Lindgren and �kerfeldt - which evoke extreme bands like Morbid Angel, the more experimental Tool, or the classic Black Sabbath, among others - and a powerful instrumental foundation alternate and blend with deep, clean vocals, crystalline acoustic elements, and Per Wiberg's hypnotic and cosmic keyboards, to construct a sonic tapestry of contrasts and shifts in intensity that moves naturally between ferocity and a hypnotic, enveloping melancholy."Ghost of Perdition", "The Baying of the Hounds" - featuring evocative Jon Lord-style organ - and the oriental-inspired "Beneath the Mire" unfold across expansive instrumental valleys and peaks that showcase the band's maturity, and find their full expression in "Reverie / Harlequin Forest" - featuring superb clean and harmonic phrasing by �kerfeldt - and, above all, in the ritualistic and intriguing "The Grand Conjuration" - reminiscent at times of Pink Floyd's "Echoes" - the album's finest moments.And the influence of "Damnation" is also present and can be felt in the tremulous "Atonement" and "Hours of Wealth," with their keyboards and a certain jazzy flair, and in the closing "Isolation Years," with its acoustic and dreamlike character, featuring �kerfeldt's whispering vocals and Lindgren's arpeggios, ultimately shaping the excellent "Ghost Reveries", one of Opeth's finest albums and standing alongside the iconic "Still Life" and "Blackwater Park".4/4.5 stars

items.body: Mara gets to Germany and does well. She earns, she buys herself a BMW, and what she boasts about is the legroom: now she can spread her legs as far as she likes. Then the car dies on the Autobahn outside Munich. The crisis has eaten her savings, the job has gone and the visa with it, and she is sat in a car she can’t afford to move. “Mara” is the first single from Gastarbeiter, the third album by GORDAN, out on Glitterbeat on 20 November. Singer Svetlana Spajić found the whole story in two lines. A bećarac, ten syllables to a line, the rhyming couplets people trade at weddings and drinking sessions in the Posavina, the farming country along the river Sava in northern Bosnia, one singer calling and another answering back, usually to make a joke or land an insult. Hers was about a woman stuck on the Autobahn in a new car with no money, sending home for someone to come and get her. Spajić wrote the rest. She keeps that couplet running through the whole lyric. Each verse says its line, then says it again with the words swapped round, Mara sliding from the end of the line into the middle. It’s a story being retold, and it gets worse every time. Halfway through, the verb shifts under the repetition and Mara stops whining that she’s been robbed and starts screaming it. By the last verse she’s home in Bosnia with none of the Deutschmarks left, back to the convertible mark, the currency Bosnia brought in after the war and fixed to the German one at one to one. Mara is a gastarbeiter, a guest worker, and there’s a whole tradition of songs about people like her. West Germany coined the word in the 1960s, after Yugoslavia broke with the rest of the socialist bloc and signed a deal to send its workers north, and it stuck in the Balkans as something said behind a man’s back. Those workers sang about missing home, about the shift, about families split by a border and parents left in the village, and that’s the body of song Gastarbeiter takes its name from. On the album sleeve is Gvozden Leaves for Temporary Residence, Mića Popović‘s painting of an ordinary Yugoslav man. Temporary residence was the state’s phrase for going to work in Germany, and Popović, a dissident, put it in the title to mock it. Gordan came together in Berlin during lockdown. Svetlana Spajić brought thirty years of going out to villages across Serbia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, learning the songs from the singers who still hold them, one place at a time, because the next valley sings the same song differently. That work has taken her into projects with Marina Abramović, Robert Wilson and Antony and the Johnsons. Austrian drummer Andi Stecher and German bassist Guido Möbius come out of noise and minimalism instead, and they also work together as GAMS. The three of them made Down in the Meadow for Morphine Records in 2021 and a self-titled album for Glitterbeat in 2024. In its own album notes, the band describes “Dark Bellow” as a dive into “instinct, desire, fear, betrayal, and rebirth,” moving through the “suffocating ghosts of hidden emotions” before closing on what the notes call “the velvet nostalgia of another life.” About Vioflesh Vioflesh formed in Santiago, Chile, at the end of 2017. The project pairs vocalist and lyricist Vio with producer Flesh. The duo works across coldwave and synthpop. darkTunes Music Group signed the band and released its debut album, “Nostalgia,” digitally on 9 May 2025. Young And Cold Records handled the vinyl edition, and Vioflesh issued its own CD and cassette pressings. The 14-track album included “Always,” “Spring Nostalgia,” “So Empty” and “Inside.” Side-Line reviewed “Nostalgia” on release, rating it 8 out of 10. Vioflesh returned with the single “Call Me” on 4 September 2026, followed by “Dark Bellow” on 2 October 2026. The band played US dates this October, including Seattle on 17 October, Portland on 21 October and San Francisco on 22 October. Ticketing listings also show European dates later in the year, including Marseille on 31 October and Rüsselsheim on 17 November, matching the band’s own note that it is “preparing to return to Europe” before the end of 2026. items.body: People leave, and time has the appalling manners to keep moving. A night of company gives way to an empty morning; the room that briefly felt habitable becomes a place for counting what has gone missing. For Obychno Odyn, that familiar collapse belongs to a much larger uncertainty, where even the smallest assurances of affection or stability can disappear before we have learned to trust them. The Turin-based coldwave and post-punk project of Ukraine expat Vadym Protsenko explores that precarious existence on the new single “Уходят люди и часы”, a title that can be translated as “People and Hours Pass.” Its accompanying video, premiering here, takes the song’s profound isolation outdoors, into tall grass, wooded paths, and the dark recesses of old stone ruins. A crunchy snare beat marches through a wash of windlike white noise before the bass establishes its brooding, melodic pattern. There is something almost reassuring about that low-end repetition, a foothold beneath a guitar line intent on making the ground uneven. Fuzzy and discordant, the guitar bends into a jagged melody with the pinched, wayward quality of an out-of-tune saxophone. Protsenko’s voice hangs farther back, its ghostly contours extended by cold reverb, as though the words have traveled across an empty building before reaching us. It makes an appropriately spectral opening to October, with enough rhythmic insistence to keep despair on its feet. The Russian-language lyrics describe a life in which direction and meaning are gradually becoming illegible. People and hours depart together, leaving little beyond the silent business of passing time. A burning planet continues to turn while everyone attends to their own concerns; words are thrown away, and even home offers no guarantee of freedom. Against that wider devastation, the possibility of being needed becomes a modest, painfully temporary refuge. The closing lines, translated into English, bring that feeling into focus: “Sometimes, we are needed by someone Sometimes, at night, we are not alone. But then the morning comes And once again, there is not a soul nearby” That repeated “Sometimes” allows a little tenderness into the song, then measures how briefly it lasts. Morning brings the return of the same absence, sharpened by having been interrupted. The bleakness comes from knowing that closeness is possible while having no confidence that it will remain. The video gives that uncertainty a grainy, unsettled physical presence. Guitar and bass performances alternate between daylight beneath the trees and murky passages enclosed by masonry. Close-ups catch faces through branches and long grass; elsewhere, the image turns upside down, briefly dislodging the performers from solid ground. The greenery crowds the frame, making these open spaces feel surprisingly secluded. There is an appealing awkwardness to the musicians’ black clothes against all that growth, as though they have brought the emotional temperature of an empty club into the middle of the afternoon. Watch the video for “Уходят люди и часы” below: Protsenko founded Obychno Odyn in Bucharest in 2025, responding to global upheaval and the situation in his home country. Writing in Russian and English, he draws on the French coldwave of the 1980s, particularly Trop Tard and Bunker Strasse. The eight-song debut album Излияние (Outpouring) followed in 2026, alongside the project’s first live performances in Bucharest, with DJ sets by Corina Sucarov. The solo project expands into a duo onstage: Protsenko handles vocals and guitar, joined by bassist Marcello Aloisio, who became part of the live lineup this year. “Уходят люди и часы” is available now on streaming platforms. items.body: Deathrock has always had a practical relationship with bad news. A macabre sense of mortality supplies the subject matter, punk supplies the impatience, and everyday life keeps renewing the subscription. East Bay four-piece Normal Weirds bring those concerns together on Frown Time, a title that sounds reasonably restrained given the circumstances. Released October 2, the band’s second full-length gathers ten songs that push further into deathpunk and deathrock while retaining their anarcho-punk roots and post-punk unease. The band’s own description, “deathrock gloom dragged through the dirt of punk,” gives a useful indication of the record’s priorities: atmosphere, abrasion, and the urgency of having something unpleasant to get off your chest. Normal Weirds released their debut album, Same Difference, in 2024, followed by the six-song EP No Lease On Life in 2025. The debut examined growing up and working free of the circumstances that had already laid out a person’s future. Taken alongside that earlier record, Frown Time suggests a widening field of concern, with individual frustration meeting the larger sense that the whole arrangement is becoming increasingly fucked. Driving basslines and hard, direct drums provide the foundation, with guitars moving between wiry punk attack and darker passages thickened by effects. Urgent, sometimes theatrical vocals heighten the unease, while lean arrangements preserve the roughness of the band’s approach. The emphasis stays on noise, tension, and the force of the playing, giving their darker direction a distinctly physical edge. The band offers Rudimentary Peni, Cemetery, T.S.O.L., and Chain Cult as points of comparison. “Deathpunk” feels like a useful shorthand for the territory they describe, where punk aggression and deathrock atmosphere share the same cramped quarters. Across their releases, Normal Weirds have increasingly brought those impulses together, giving the darker material a harder and more direct frame. Mortality, alienation, and everyday absurdity run through the album’s lyrical concerns. Its ominous mood draws on both personal experience and a broader disillusionment with the present. There is a bluntness to the title that suits that outlook: Frown Time makes room for the irritation and apprehension people are often expected to swallow while getting on with their day. Frown Time was recorded, mixed, and produced by Skot Brown of Altar De Fey and mastered by Greg Wilkinson. The album is available to stream and purchase on Bandcamp here. It will be released on other streaming platforms, excluding Spotify, on October 16, 2026. items.body: Somewhere between the panic attack and the curtain call, Fiona’s Phobias have found a rather entertaining place to set up shop. Their six-track EP DEMOnS Vol. 1 dresses burnout, self-disgust, and impossible attachments in gothic metal, pop punk, and dark cabaret, with enough theatrical excess to suggest that the orchestra pit has opened directly into hell. The jokes have teeth, the guitars favor elaborate flourishes, and the people inside these songs keep discovering that their favorite distractions have become further reasons to worry. Formed in 2022, the project pairs the deliberately elusive Nikki L with vocalist Krisanna Marie, whose background includes Hatesex, Penis Flytrap, and burlesque fire Go-Go performance. Their own comparison of the working relationship to The Phantom of the Opera seems appropriate for music so fond of trapdoors and dramatic entrances. Marie’s ability to move from a knowing, almost conversational delivery into operatic gestures gives these elaborate arrangements a useful center: someone has to keep an eye on the audience while the scenery catches fire. Euphoria is Tragic starts with a chugging guitar figure planted between punk and metal, while Marie brings a retro rock directness to its catalogue of procrastination and depleted pleasure. Around the minute mark, the arrangement grows dense with baroque embellishment; a wiry solo takes on something of an electric violin’s bite. The bright momentum makes an effective companion to lyrics about getting bored with your own bad habits. “I feel my powers wane; a witch without her magic” supplies the perfect image for that particular exhaustion, when yesterday’s magnificent escape becomes today’s inability to answer an email. The theatrical scale expands on Play It Cool, which sets an almost lounge-like opening vocal against metal accents before breaking into a gallop. There is something of Malice Mizer’s baroque grandeur in the meeting of ornate arrangements and vocal melodrama, with the forward motion suggesting the carriage from Castlevania: Rondo of Blood racing toward Dracula’s front door. Beneath the spectacle lies a grimly familiar instruction: take your pill, eat your food, behave, and convince everyone that nothing is wrong. As Marie’s singing becomes more operatic, the pressure to appear composed turns increasingly sinister, eventually spilling into the song’s bloodied escape fantasy. Imaginary Sins brings piano, nimble bass, and busy drums into a crooked little cabaret before the heavier ornamentation takes over. Guitar flourishes answer the rhythm’s clipped figures, and goblin-like responses jostle Marie’s lead, as though every unwanted thought has secured a speaking part. Its funniest lyric finds the bodily absurdity inside a familiar wish: “Wishin’ I was pretty on the inside – But there’s just guts.” Jealousy, appetite, and self-absorption populate this ballroom of dancing demons, while the music’s constant activity makes obsession feel exhausting even at its most playful. The cover of Bang Bang, offered as an ode to Kill Bill, fits neatly among these accounts of love going horribly wrong. A Phantom-style organ opening and old-school metal guitar melody send the song toward the grand, charging territory of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero. Its childhood games and adult abandonment acquire the dimensions of a stage tragedy, complete with an ornate guitar solo. Placed between the EP’s psychological grotesques, the familiar tune becomes another example of affection leaving somebody flat on the floor. Whispers and giallo-like synth tones introduce She Loves To Kiss That Doll, before sweeping guitars open the room around Marie’s voice. An operatic interlude, edged with chimes, suspends the heavier movement as she sings of attachment to a figure whose beauty depends on a terrible act of denial. Stuffing, cold hands, and the replacement of blood with a handsome face turn romantic idealization into physical horror. The return of the metal arrangement gives that revelation force, while the lyric’s eventual admission that he has long been dead makes the tenderness more disturbing than any decorative cobweb could manage. Closing track Bittersweet Darling begins with chilly piano and the worn texture of an old recording, then carries that melodic idea into a broad sweep of gothic guitar. Progressive tempo changes unsettle a romance conducted through black-and-white television images, broken mirrors, and the comfort of a boxed-up illusion. Its lover remains available because the screen can keep performing; the person watching has surrendered something harder to recover. By the final turn toward the knife and the closing credits, the song has brought the EP’s appetite for spectacle into uncomfortable proximity with self-destruction. Across DEMOnS Vol. 1, the sheer amount of decoration can crowd the stage, but Marie’s shifts in delivery and the songs’ sharply drawn situations keep the excess purposeful. Fiona’s Phobias are especially effective when a grotesque image exposes an ordinary humiliation: craving attention while avoiding people, mistaking possession for love, or spending all your energy on the thing that leaves you empty. They have given those contradictions a lavish production, and the casting department appears to have found plenty of monsters willing to sing. DEMOnS Vol. 1 is out now, released October 2 via Misophoniac Rabbit. Listen below and find the EP on Bandcamp and Spotify. items.body: Neram Pularumbol (“As The Dawn Breaks”) finds Sunken Cages pulling the rhythmic traditions of South India into an electronic vocabulary of bass, drones, and fractured club music. The album opens in celebratory, ebullient mode with “Kerala”, before “Elephant Dance” raises the tempo and “Idakka” takes a more synthetic path, processing patterns from the traditional hourglass-shaped Kerala drum. Breath soon becomes almost as important as rhythm. On “Darantee”, featuring Kuza, vocal exhalations and percussion give the music a physicality that draws on the agricultural and folk roots of South India. The connection with Kerala runs throughout the record, particularly through the collective force of its percussion traditions. “Drum and Flowers” imagines Chenda drums within a celebratory night dance, their increasingly animated rhythms rubbing against darker industrial sounds. “Athiraavile” — Malayalam for “early in the morning” or “at the break of dawn” — shifts the scene towards daybreak, combining an unprocessed Chenda melam pattern with heavy electronic beats and Rani Jambak’s incantatory voice. Throughout, traditional instruments remain clearly audible even as their rhythmic properties are stretched, fragmented and repositioned. The second half effectively takes that process apart again through a substantial series of remixes. “Drum and Flowers” alone appears in three new iterations: Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull its rhythmic framework in sharply different directions, at points veering towards acid, jungle and deconstructed club music. The source material consequently keeps changing hands and contexts, with each version exposing possibilities latent in the original. For all its electronic density, Neram Pularumbol eventually circles back towards the physical act of playing. “Kerala (Moki McFly Remix)” brings proceedings to an apt conclusion, returning percussion to a more tactile foreground and introducing distinctly jazzy, free-form leanings. The album begins and ends with “Kerala”, but the intervening transformations ensure that the return doesn’t feel quite like arriving at the same place. photo by Mike Vanemon To find out more about the production process for the album, we got in touch directly with Ravish Momin (aka Sunken Cages). The liner notes to Neram Pularumbol use resynthesis not simply as an electronic process but as a metaphor for taking culture apart into its constituent elements and putting it together differently, in opposition to the idea of tradition as something “frozen, solidified and sanctified”. That does seem particularly audible on Neram Pularumbol, where South Indian instruments and rhythmic languages are present but rarely allowed to function as straightforward markers of heritage. What exactly are you trying to preserve when you dismantle and reconstruct a tradition in this way, and at what point does transformation become more important than recognisability? Does this also connect with what you have described elsewhere as “resynthesizing the traditional” and decolonising conventional ideas of so-called global music? Thanks for this great question! The best analogy to start with is to think of making a photocopy of a photocopy. Even 8-10 generations of copies later, they do not resemble the original, get distorted and warped, and perhaps even a new narrative emerges. This process itself is of deep interest to me and what I’m hoping to preserve. When I think of a rhythm I’ve learned in the past, it’s more about how I’m recalling it in the moment, with all the unconscious inspirations and changes that get added over time- to be left with a transformation that’s an impression, an organic reimagining- similar to what happens to our own memories over time. Furthermore, I’m taking these ‘resynthesized patterns’ and placing them in a new framework of synths, drones, and other electronic elements that I’ve absorbed, to create a new global-music that simply doesn’t rely on invoking the past. I need to be careful to add that all this does not mean a blatant disrespect of the culture and tradition, but to be left with recognizable elements-like the sounds and basic structure of a pattern- in an arrangement that may be unfamiliar. That’s where the decolonizing takes shape. Music is predicated on a dynamic process of growth and evolution, yet too often non-western artists are expected to be performative of their culture, and their use of contemporary technologies or drawing inspirations from western genres is considered disingenuous. Gatekeeping and branding from western ethnomusicologists and curators has a long problematic history, but I’ll leave that discussion for another time Neram Pularumbol is particularly rooted in the musical traditions of Kerala, from the title itself to “Idakka”, named after the hourglass-shaped drum associated with Kerala’s temple music. Yet you don’t present these traditions ethnographically or attempt to reproduce them faithfully: their rhythmic and timbral characteristics are broken apart and absorbed into electronics, bass and club structures. Which particular Kerala musical traditions, instruments or rhythmic practices fed into this album, and what is your own relationship to them? Are there elements that you consciously wanted to retain in recognisable form, and others that you felt could only remain alive by being transformed? Hopefully my previous response lends some insight to this question as well. To elaborate, I’ve always found group drumming to be powerful, an action of resistance and solidarity as well as of spiritual significance. Particularly, I was mesmerized by music performances known as Chenda melam in which hundreds of artists sync and perform together during temple festivals in Kerala. The drums native to Kerala, like the Chenda, Idakka and Elathalam, also have markedly different timbres/sonorities from the North-Indian drums such as Tabla and Dhol to which one may be accustomed to hearing. While I’m originally from South India (Hyderabad) myself, I currently split my time between Brooklyn and Philadelphia. I did not grow up in Kerala, India, but I wanted to think about what a meaningful recreation of those rituals into my own worldview, that was culturally respectful as well, would represent. For example, On “Drum and Flowers,” I created a narrative with shifting tempos where the Chenda drum is used in a celebratory night dance, after the workers have come home. A multitude of drums lead the celebrations, shedding industrial grime for synchronized movements that quicken, a shared bodily memory of ancestral resistance and resilience. The song is punctuated with industrial textures and dark synth stabs that represent the rigor of factory-work. “Idakka,” the track to which you’d alluded earlier, runs the Idakka drum patterns through various delays and echo filters to create this cavernous rhythmic feel where machine-like sounds are also ever-present. Here the traditional elements are drastically transformed and chopped up, signifying a not-too-distant future where machines threaten to take over humanity. On “Athiraavile,” which features the Indonesian producer/vocalist Rani Jambak, I actually used a clean / unprocessed Chenda melam pattern on top of heavy electronic beats. Here, Rani lends a shaman-like call to prayer- not belonging to any specific religious denomination- where people gather to play drums at dawn. The second half of the album effectively allows other artists to take your rhythmic material apart again. “Drum and Flowers” is especially revealing because Weldroid, Lila Tirando a Violeta and El Kontessa pull the same source towards very different rhythmic and electronic environments, while Masma Dream World and Moki McFly produce two strikingly different versions of “Kerala” and Kush Arora makes “Idakka” considerably harsher and more propulsive. You have said that these collaborators were chosen partly through relationships you have built with artists around the world who approach tradition as something mutable rather than fixed. When you heard the finished remixes, did any of them reveal something in your own compositions that you hadn’t realised was there? And does handing the music over to artists from such different cultural and musical contexts become another stage of the album’s idea of resynthesis? The remixes were as much a part of the album as the tracks. And a resounding yes to your observation of having these remixes represent a further reshaping of the source-material, as multiple layers of resynthesis now exist Each artist brought their respective cultural background, musical aesthetic and production style to the table. Back during the pandemic lockdown in 2020, I’d actively sought out remote collaborations with artists in different corners of the globe. I do want to emphasize that it was also important for me to support women artists, do my part to highlight them in a male-dominated electronic music scene. Over the years, I’ve maintained my goal of building a musical community with diverse collaborators who all take musical risks and blend the traditional to the digital in their own practice. As an artist with a remix track-record of my own (Babani Sound System, Batida’s Ikoqwe, Depeche Mode, dragonchild and Thollem), I’ve spent a lot of time listening to a given track to quickly hone in on elements that resonated with my aesthetic- whether it was a vocal phrase, a melody or a rhythmic motif. The objective was to take apart the original track and re-stitch it back together highlighting that chosen element, in ways that wouldn’t be predictable. El Kontessa added a doumbek pattern to the underlying rhythm and made it feel like it was always there, as if South Indian and Egyptian musicians jammed all the time. Masma Dream World took the drone elements of “Kerala” which I’d intentionally layered heavily, to create a very cinematic track with a stripped down minimal beat. Weldroid’s acid synths and bit-crushed elements gave the track a dance music of the future energy. Lila Tirando a Violeta removed my rhythmic elements entirely and energized the track with a Jungle vibe. Moki Mc Fly seemed to instinctively grasp my AACM past- which was grounded in their ancient to the future motto- and brought an acoustic Free-Jazz tribute to the Art Ensemble of Chicago to his remix. Neram Pularumbol means “As The Dawn Breaks”, while the name Sunken Cages itself has a much darker environmental origin: you have described the “sunken cage” as an image of something once held captive becoming submerged by rising waters, reflecting your background in environmental engineering and longstanding concern with climate change. Yet this record often feels less apocalyptic than that image suggests: despite the drones, industrial textures and moments of considerable darkness, there is movement, colour and a sense of emergence. What does “dawn” mean within this record? Is it intended as a counterweight to the darker implications of Sunken Cages, or do you see destruction, transformation and renewal as parts of the same process? For the past few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the duality of the nature of water, as a source of survival and also as one of destruction. While there is a sense of hopelessness that comes from realizing that some of the impacts of climate-change are irreversible, there is also hope in focussing on environmentally sustainable practices. Rather than thinking of dawn as a counterweight to the bleakness of the overarching climate narrative, I wanted to leave its symbolism ambiguous. In other words, we can meet the dawn feeling powerless or prepare to transform our future for preservation. On a broader level, the choice still doesn’t seem to have been made. As far as the tracks go, I play with the tension between the forces of darkness and rejuvenation- with the industrial sounds/textures on the verge of overpowering the ancient rhythms and chants, which signify our humanity, and certainly different tracks allude to different outcomes of that struggle. PS. Since this interview took place, Momin has released Morning Birds and Distant Drums, a new album with Haitian “soundchemist” Val Jeanty as Turning Jewels Into Water. Taking the AACM credo “Ancient to the Future” as a guiding principle, the record brings their Indian and Haitian lineages into a kinetic dialogue with improvisation and contemporary electronics. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Pekka Streng's music is colored by his personal history, much like the stories of Tim Buckley or Nick Drake, singer-songwriters who passed away prematurely. Perhaps unconsciously, they gravitated toward that deeply intimate, heart-wrenching subgenre, the folk singer-songwriter, in which an artist reveals so much of themselves. He was accompanied by musicians from the Finnish jazz scene, such as Eero Koivistoinen and Pekka P�yry (on saxophone and flute, respectively); both would later participate in bassist Pekka Pohjola's album Harakka Bialoipokku (1974)."Mimosaneito" ventures into jazz, yet the mood shifts to something more intimate and reflective on "Kaukana." Pekka possessed the power to transport us out of our reality through the sheer magic of his vocal timbre; like singer-songwriters such as Donovan, he commanded a rich stylistic range, shifting between psychedelic, acoustic, jazz-inflected, and ethereal sounds, to enter that mythological realm which, at times during the 60s and 70s, felt so real it was almost tangible.From the groove-laden pop of the track ...Ja Tuittu Ruusut Sai to a blues piece with a touch of rustic country in Perhonen. However, it was Pekka's more mystical, mysterious, and inspired side that truly shone when he sang in Finnish, performing tracks like Auringon Lapsi that evoked distant, almost medieval, times, as if they had reached us through oral tradition. It was also reminiscent of the early days of Tyrannosaurus Rex, when Marc Bolan favored an acoustic sound and explored Eastern and psychedelic influences.As for the title, it alludes to the land in summer, when everything bursts into color and blooms; the summer solstice is precisely when Juhannus is celebrated in Finland, a time when people traditionally headed to the lakes throughout June. Both the cover art and the music convey something of this spirit. It ranges from a dark organ solo on "Kanttorinpoika Max" to the magical "Katsele Y�ss�," featuring only Pekka's voice, his guitar, and a rather Baroque-style sopranino saxophone solo.Roope Hattu reminded me of the freshness and freedom of Bob Dylan's bluesy "The Man in Me", though this was the Finnish version, transformed by Jukka Ruohom�ki's synthesizers into a kind of cosmic blues, evolving from the style of The Band (Dylan's friends and collaborators) into something otherworldly. "Puutarhassa" sports a very welcome bossa nova vibe that lends itself well to the acoustic format and the album's stylistic, and emotional, variety, shifting from the optimism of a sunny day... to the introspection of a gray, rainy one, if we are talking about stereotypes, that is. Though certainly not musical ones."Mutta Min� L�hden" is curiously divided into two parts: one acoustic, featuring guitar, and another with vocals and the celesta, that instrument created by the French harmonium maker Auguste Mustel. Resembling a glockenspiel, it takes us by surprise not only with its sweetness but also with its brevity; it is a piece filled with ambivalence, yet one that leaves us certain we have heard a genuine expression of the artist's own voice.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if setting out to provide a soundtrack for the atmosphere of their native Finland, with snowflakes falling and blanketing everything in White, Horte crafts a hypnotic soundscape using electronic elements and synthesizers. They create a downtempo vibe that occasionally flirts with Portishead-style trip-hop, yet later reveals a folk-hop intimacy reminiscent of The Beta Band.Vocalist Riikka Pekkala's voice seems to float, notably on the opening track, "Pelko Karistaa J'rjen," where echoes reverberate as "Ilman Nurkka" unfolds amidst samples and loops, sung in their native tongue. In an album defined by wintry textures and a palette of blues and whites, the track "Kilpemme" seems to mimic a thaw amidst guttural guitar sounds, evoking a sense of Nordic psychedelia. It is a landscape where we lose ourselves like early polar explorers illuminated by the aurora borealis; a rock sensibility permeates the electronic modernity of this unhurried atmosphere, frozen like a block of ice that preserves the life within, holding it in suspended animation, paradoxically enough."Valoa On Liikaa" seems to mark time like a clock; Riikka Pekkala's voice takes center stage, conveying a stark, pale quality that nonetheless carries an inherent strength. Repetition, acting much like a metronome, sets an unwavering rhythm for the vocal variations. It is at this point that the synthesizer evokes string sounds and an emotional peak occurs, as the opposing poles converge."The Earth Gives Silence to the Night" is a highly evocative title for the album; "Kun Joki Haihtuu" is a powerful track where the bass and drums kick in, as if they had been waiting for the moment to break the ice and shatter it into crystals. These are moods that music used to express differently, perhaps never before so raw and stripped-down, revealing nature itself at that precise instant when everything comes to a standstill."V'isty Tielt'" is the most rock-oriented track, yet it defies convention; it leans into a kind of Krautrock-style transgression where Riikka Pekkala's vocals, clean and pure, almost like a religious plea, contrast sharply with a gritty, powerful backing track that advances with a "scorched-earth" strategy, leaving nothing in its wake. As one of the album's most progressive tracks, everything here sounds analog; there even seems to be a Mellotron-style choir, despite no actual Mellotron being used, though the sound is certainly processed to evoke that effect. The highly groovy bassline plays a pivotal role, transforming the song into a prophetic experience."Konttaa, Ne Konttaa II" brings the album to a close with echoes and Riikka's voice promising an eternal return, the certainty that things remain in motion despite appearing motionless, like the trees and all the surrounding nature of which we, of course, are a part.

items.body: Review by Logan — The ambient, coolly nostalgic opening sequence of Geogaddi indicates the record's direction. Adjusting to the full album required some acclimation after years of listening to Music Has the Right to Children, but many elements appealed to me right away. Taking some distance from the debut allowed this strange, isolated world to make sense."Music Is Math" and "1969" rely on steady, ticking beats reminiscent of the D�sseldorf electronic scene, but with an uneasy feeling underneath. Further into the tracklist, pieces like "The Beach at Redpoint", "Gyroscope", and "Alpha and Omega" shift toward a darker Krautrock friction. The record relies on hypnotic, repetitive loops rather than traditional musical showmanship, focusing on old-sounding, distorted analog textures.My first favourite was clearly Music Has the Right to Children, which I found immediately accessible, followed by The Campfire Headphase, though I still loved Geogaddi during that era. However, it was only after Inferno came out that I deeply loved the final three albums, and the early material became more distant to me. This record is more like a 4.5 for me, though it gets a rounded-down 4 for Prog Archives purposes. Geogaddi is a strong exercise in sound design, but it remains a step below those late-career masterpieces for me. Inferno, The Campfire Headphase, and Tomorrow's Harvest mean the most to me these days, but all of Boards of Canada's albums I consider to be masterpieces in their own ways.Key tracks for me: "The Beach at Redpoint" and "Music is Math".

Yet we are rediscovering music of undeniable quality and originality. Over time, CARDIACS has evolved from an unclassifiable oddity to a legendary band, recognized by virtually everyone (including the British press, which is no stranger to belated revivals) as a major piece of the global rock puzzle.*On Land And In The Sea* follows in the footsteps of its predecessor (*A Little Man And A House ...*, 1988), offering art-rock laced with frenzied madness, but this time without the element of surprise and with, in its first half, a more pronounced "prunk" vibe?the merry band having saved the best for last with "Buds and Spawn," a psychedelic anthem that could have been dreamed up in 1968 by a Syd Barrett even more unhinged than usual; and above all "The Everso Closely Guarded Line," a grandiose psycho-symphonic epic owed in part to Drake, which moves forward through an electric haze to the sounds of solemn keyboards. Sarah's sudden departure in the spring of 1989 (she would continue to collaborate sporadically with Tim Smith for a few more years) and, above all, that of William D. Drake two years later marked the end of an era. Drake was not replaced, and Tim Smith took sole charge of the keyboards, which were henceforth less prominent.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Is CARDIACS a progressive rock band? The question, which may have sparked debate at one time, seems obsolete today. All we can say is that singer and guitarist Tim Smith?the band's longtime leader, its heart, mind, and soul, and now more than ever regarded as an exceptional English artist, more than five years after his passing?is a child of the vibrant prog universe that truly lives up to its name. He himself cited among his countless influences such legendary names as Genesis, Faust, Can, Gong, Zappa, and Gentle Giant?a fact confirmed by the album *A Little Man And A House And The Whole World Window*.From the very introduction of the excellent new version of the track "A Little Man and a House," it becomes clear that this album will be on an entirely different level than *Seaside*, their previous album released in 1983. The compositions date back to the previous three years, but the production is much richer than on *Seaside* and in no way tainted by the typical sound of the '80s. Musically, it's a true leap forward, with arrangements of unprecedented richness ("The Icing on the World"), sometimes bordering on unnecessary excess ("The Breakfast Line," saved by its impressive grand finale). The significant contribution of William D. Drake's keyboards (who joined the band in late 1983) is no small part of this, as the musician displays a boundless imagination that rivals Tim's. Drake also co-wrote two of the album's most progressive tracks: "I'm Eating in Bed," which appears as a bonus track?a surreal little nursery rhyme that could easily have fit on *Nursery Cryme* or *Foxtrot*; and "The Whole World Window," which closes the album in a rather unexpected way, bringing CARDIACS closer to King Crimson's *In The Court* with heavy use of mellotron, piano, and bombastic organ, thereby convincing us once and for all that this is one of the most important prog works of 1988.

items.body: Review by Lewian — It is somewhat frustrating about rock from the old communist GDR (East Germany) that the possibilityof censorship didn't only affect the lyrics but apparently also had an impact on the music itself.People were strongly discouraged to think outside the box, and also to sound outside the box. Soproper innovation was very hard to find if at all. Everyone apparently wanted to (or had to) soundnice and civilised. In the 70s it was possible to play harder rock music if it clearly referenced,copied or covered rock'n roll and blues from the west as this was seen as anti western establishmentrebellion and therefore OK (at least at a certain time point), but rebellion against the ownconditions of life in the east wasn't allowed. This also meant that anything more aggressive anddark couldn't be done in innovative ways and couldn't directly relate to the musicians' daily life,seriously affecting creativity. Any opposition had to be subtle, often covered by nice melodicmusic, often enough straight and easy to listen to, and often of little attraction to the proglistener 40 years or so later. Lyrics were often poetic and indirect. Innovation could be brought in best by incorporating classical musicinfluences, as Electra and Stern Meissen did, and Lift to some extent. I believe that the situationfor creativity was really more problematic in the GDR than it was for example in Poland, Hungary andthe Czech Republic, but I can't know for sure (certainly there was a more lively jazz scene in thelatter countries).Lift's Meeresfahrt is one of the best albums to negotiate these conditions. It is in factastonishing that the major theme of longing for travel and far away countries on this album didn'tcreate problems with the censors, as far as I know, given that most people were not allowed totravel outside the eastern communist block of countries. The album is very melodic indeed, the band doesn't rock hard (OK a little bit in very few places),but they are good at what they do. Most arrangements are dominated by the two very good keyboarders.The vocals are also attractive, clean and melodic. The opener "Wir fahrn uebers Meer" is an exampleof copying western blues rock. Maybe the band used this to distract the censors, because in my viewit is by far the weakest track. This is followed by the extremely beautiful "Nach Sueden" ("GoSouth"). Not the proggiest track, but featuring a wonderful melody, a strong keyboard part, andlyrics on migrating birds that probably expressed the longing of many young people in the GDR butwere seemingly (and surprisingly) innocent enough for the censors to let the band get away withthis. A highlight!"Scherbenglas" is an example for the classical influence, using only a string section and voice. Norock at all but interesting and not bad. "Tagesreise" has an epic melody and works well asrecommendation piece for the prog fan with some contrasts and several sections. The second highlightof the album.On the B-side, "Meeresfahrt" (something like "Journey at Sea") is the longest track. It developsslowly from calm keyboards into a mostly instrumental journey featuring the keyboarders andsaxophonist in particular. This is surely enjoyable even though it may be a bit too long for what itis. "Sommernacht" is a calm good night song referencing traditional singing. It works well asending, even though not very interesting from the instrumental point of view. "Tagesreise" and "Meeresfahrt" hold most interest from the prog point of view, but the album hasvery nice elements also elsewhere if you are into melodic rock. It has light influences fromclassical music, jazz and blues. It has good variety but also comes over as consistent featuring acharacteristic style, particularly the melodies and keyboards. The most similar band I can think of is Novalis. Personally I'd rank this as thesecond best GDR prog/art rock album (after Stern Meissen's Reise zum Mittelpunkt des Menschen). 3.7stars.Sadly, few months after the release of this album in 1978, band members Henry Pacholski and GerhardZachar died in a traffic accident and the band would never be the same anymore.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Quivira?the legendary name of a city of gold, forever sought but never found!It is also the concept behind an album by Lisa LaRue, who shines on keyboards and piano.1. (Intro) "The Coming Of The Spaniards" offers a symphonic, solemn, and majestic opening?a melody that stops you in your tracks. The choirs, the piano, the very essence of the music?simply perfect.2. "The Benefits Of Breathing Quietly" follows, featuring Vangelis-esque tones?sublime, with a distant, Native American-inspired breeze. Jake's vocals flirt with the style of Big Big Train; in short, top-tier stuff. The synth kicks in, riding over violin-like tones; it's simple yet beautiful, with hints of Alan Parsons?nothing but quality here.3. "The Plains? Truth" features a slow, drifting violin in "space-folk" mode?an airy instrumental interlude?concluding with an Andalusian acoustic touch that remains captivating throughout.4. "Quivira Bound" places the keyboard center stage; Jake casts a spell with his distinctive voice?not the late John, certainly, but his vocals are pure prog. It's an 80s-style ballad with a cheerful air; Lisa brings out a smaller synth before a Southern-rock/Cherokee guitar spirit floods the room with bewitching notes, with John embracing his role as an ex-Korgis member. A stereo finale blends the organ with the crystalline piano.5. "Moving Forward" reminds me of Solstice, featuring a jazzy-folk sound where Joe's violin engages in a musical duel. KANSAS is definitely present here after all, and the keyboards blend perfectly for one of the album's surprising detours.6. "The Turk/Follow The Wind" follows with organ, piano, and violin?sampled or not? That is the question. The drums aren't credited, implying they are programmed, which takes a bit of the shine off the album. Otherwise, it's a fine, energetic track that would have been a hit in the 70s! The cinematic ending puts my mind at ease.7. "Nothing Is Everything" marks the second half of the album?Side B. It has that KANSAS vibe again, with plenty of piano; softer yet dynamic, it feels like an 80s tune?over 40 years old; is it impossible to invent something new these days? Anyway, at times I hear ALAN PARSONS in "Andalusian mode"?it's a strange sensation.8. "Carved From The Sun," with its warm organ, reminds me of SHADOW GALLERY?that's just how it is. The velvety keyboard work lets the track drift along a smooth, seamless melodic path?paradoxically so.9. "Kicking Rocks" arrives, driven by a catchy guitar and a heavy riff; then it settles back down for a repeat performance.10. "Prelude To Anywhere/Weekend Conquistadors"... is it the spellbinding piano, the violin, or the synth? A beautiful ballad assaulted by John's hard-rocking riff, with the piano returning to sweep away any lingering heaviness. A masterful battle between the two instruments?top-tier stuff?with Jake setting things on fire, as does the PROTO-KAW-style vocal.11. "Still Breathing," with notes that recall TEARS FOR FEARS?that's just how it is. The final track; instead of leaving me breathless, it fills me up. A ballad?a lament balancing tenderness and emotion?featuring a violin? a keyboard? building to a dreamlike crescendo that drifts away on the musical breeze. A touch of Alan Parsons once again highlights the profound musicality of this final, spellbinding track. Off you go, steed?scram!QUIVIRA: symphonic progressive rock; a modern myth and vision of our troubled society set to music; melodic instrumental prog with occasional vocals?very good, yet it also tends to go in circles. Mr. Cadbury really shouldn't have wandered in.(3.75)

items.body: Harry Birch wrote “Don’t Give Up” while he was drinking himself under and his mother was dying of bone cancer. “This song saved me,” he says. He wrote it for her. The music pulls against all that: warm bass, guitar ringing bright over it, the tempo unhurried. Only the first line gives it away, Birch calling himself “a whiskey walking junkie”. Halfway through the song, he hands a verse to Lunda, a French-Congolese singer working in soul and indie rock. The chorus asks for time to put a broken life back together: “Please don’t give up on me / ‘Cause oh on our love we can revive / the pieces of our life…” Birch is Kaya Street, the Bristol project he writes, sings and produces. He formed it in 2014 as a ten-piece soul band, broke it up in early 2024 to get into the studio properly, then rebuilt it at the end of that year around live horns, drums and electronics. Juno-winning Toronto producer Dubmatix is producing the next Kaya Street album. “Don’t Give Up” stands apart from the afrobeat he usually works in, and from the political songs that come with it. items.body: Pygmy Children reissue their 1994 debut album “Malignant” as “Malignant: Redux” via Re:Mission Entertainment. The label describes the release as electro-industrial and EBM, with a release date of October 2, 2026. The original “Malignant” was recorded by Brian Roper and Pete Roper at Hit And Run Studios in Rockville, Maryland, between September and December 1993, and released on CD via Noname/Noslogan Productions in 1994 with an 11-track listing running from “Shock V3.1” through “File Regarding…”. “Malignant: Redux” adds five further tracks to that original running order. Re:Mission Entertainment has not published a description of what the “Redux” edition changes beyond its expanded tracklist; that detail is not yet confirmed. Malignant : Redux by Pygmy Children About Pygmy Children Pygmy Children is a US electro-industrial project built around Brian Roper and Pete Roper, active since the early 1990s. The duo released their debut album “Malignant” in 1994, followed by “Low Life Dream” in 1998. After a long gap, Pygmy Children returned through Re:Mission Entertainment with the EP “I Have No Name”, the single “Proof in Lies”, the “Signal Unknown” EP and the album “Coincidental Strategies”. “Malignant: Redux”, out October 2, 2026, revisits the project’s debut album more than three decades after its original release.

The album is inspired by the music of John Foxx and Die Form. “Tristesse” explores the fragile human psyche, where anger and melancholy sit next to each other. items.body: Vampire Valentine release “Scarred & Sacred” on October 25, 2026 via Morella Records. The six-track EP is the UK darkwave and post-punk trio’s fourth release since signing to the label on January 15, 2026, following a run of singles, the “Pale Dawn” EP and their self-titled debut album this past August. Where the self-titled album was a complete statement of the band’s sound, “Scarred & Sacred” follows a single arc across its six tracks: sin, repentance and the reckoning that waits at the gate. “Scarred & Sacred is our sins repenting and facing your fate in the afterlife at the gate,” the band says. “We wanted six tracks that felt like one story, not six songs that happened to ship together. It starts calm and it does not stay that way.” Scarred & Sacred tracklist Scarred (instrumental) – an atmospheric, melodic intro that turns unsettling, setting up the EP. Broken Sins – a full-length track pairing darkwave production with post-punk revival. Talisman – the story of a lover placing a talisman with a dying partner to guide them to the other side. Lover Not A Biter (instrumental) – a hard-driven darksynth track. GORE! (instrumental) – a darksynth cut the band describes as built on 1980s horror soundtracks and visuals. Sacred – the title track and closer, a post-punk song ending on vocals from frontman Michael Longstaff. Credits Michael Longstaff handles lyrics and vocals, Kieron Wright plays bass and Tobias Cowen Pickard plays drums. Tony Gunk produced, composed, mixed and mastered all six tracks. Ricky Conover, who records as Forerunnerx, co-produced and co-composed “Scarred”, “Lover Not A Biter” and “GORE!”. Blake Carpenter plays guitar on “Broken Sins”, “Talisman”, “Lover Not A Biter” and “GORE!”. About Vampire Valentine Vampire Valentine is a darkwave and post-punk band from Newcastle upon Tyne, formed in October 2025 by producer Michael Longstaff and bassist/guitarist Kieron Wright, who connected through a mutual acquaintance, along with drummer Tobias Cowen Pickard. US producers Ricky Conover (Forerunnerx) and Tony Gunk handle production. The band draws on The Sisters of Mercy, Twin Tribes, She Past Away and Lebanon Hanover. They debuted on November 14, 2025 with the single “Porcelain”, backed with “Olivia”, which goth journalist Mick Mercer called an “Excellent Debut”. A second single, “Thorns”, followed on December 1, 2025. Vampire Valentine signed to Morella Records on January 15, 2026 and released their debut full-length album that August, having already shared the singles “In The Dark” and “Cutting Ties” from it. “Scarred & Sacred”, out October 25, follows as the band’s fourth Morella release in under a year.

items.body: Test Dept and the Welsh performance company Brith Gof release “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” on 4 December 2026 via Artoffact Records. The set expands their 1989 album into a 3CD/1DVD box, alongside a separate red vinyl LP and a digital edition. “Gododdin” is based on Y Gododdin, the earliest surviving Welsh-language poem, written around 600 AD. It tells of 300 Celtic warriors who attacked 100,000 invading Angles and lost. Test Dept and Brith Gof first staged the piece as a live performance at an abandoned Rover car factory in Cardiff in December 1988, using 600 tons of sand, 50 trees and 30 wrecked cars on a set that flooded as the show went on. Further performances followed in 1989 in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The original 1989 studio album was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios from Test Dept’s existing studio and field recordings, augmented with brass and wind courtesy of Brith Gof’s John E R Hardy and bagpipes from Alistair Adams. Paul Jamrozy’s voice runs alongside the Welsh-language vocals of Lis Hughes Jones. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” widens that original 7-track album with 19 tracks that have not previously been released. The first disc is a reworked version built from newly unearthed multitrack tapes of the early studio sessions, put together by Test Dept founder members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy during the summer of 2026. The second disc carries a live recording from one of the 1989 performances, staged in a quarry in Polverigi, Italy. The DVD holds a documentary from the period, with live footage and interviews with performers, academics and other experts. Compiled by Test Dept with input from Brith Gof members Lis Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms, the set was remastered by Paul Lavigne at Kontrast Mastering. It comes in a 5-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet of archival imagery and writing, including an essay by author and Test Dept researcher Alexei Monroe. The artwork for both the box and the separate red vinyl LP was redesigned by Paul Jamrozy and Stefan Alt (ant-zen); the vinyl edition carries the original album plus one previously unreleased track and a printed insert. Ahead of the box set, Test Dept released the advance single “Gwr a Aeth Gatraeth / Prologue (Early Studio Sessions, Reworked 2026)” on 2 October 2026, available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” is the second in Test Dept’s ongoing series of archival reissues on Artoffact Records, who signed the band in 2025 for catalogue reissues and a new album. It follows the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, released a year earlier. Artoffact will also release new Test Dept material in 2027. A separate event ties into the reissue: Test Dept and Brith Gof take part in a discussion and Q&A about “Gododdin” at Chapter in Cardiff on 24 October, as part of the Experimentica festival’s 25th-anniversary programme. About Test Dept Test Dept formed in London in the early 1980s as an industrial music group built around live percussion on scrap metal and found objects. In 1988 and 1989, the band collaborated with the Welsh avant-garde theatre company Brith Gof on “Gododdin”, staging it first at an abandoned car factory in Cardiff and then on tour in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. The 1989 studio album version was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios. Test Dept returned to active release and performance in the 2020s. In 2025, the band signed to Artoffact Records for a series of catalogue reissues alongside a new studio album. The first of those reissues, the 4xCD “Industrial Overture: Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”, arrived in October 2025. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster”, out 4 December 2026, is the second. Current members Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy built new versions of the early “Gododdin” studio sessions for the reissue during the summer of 2026, working from recently unearthed multitrack tapes. Test Dept continue to tour, with confirmed UK and European dates running from October 2026 into the summer of 2027, and have a new studio album due via Artoffact in 2027. About Brith Gof Brith Gof is a Welsh performance company known for large-scale, site-specific theatre work that drew on Welsh history and language. Co-founded by figures including Mike Pearson, Lis Hughes Jones and Clifford McLucas, the company staged “Gododdin” with Test Dept in Cardiff in 1988, adapting the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin into a promenade performance inside a disused car factory. Hughes Jones, John E R Hardy and Heike Roms were directly involved in compiling “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” alongside Test Dept.

Miss Construction’s road back to ‘This Is Crap’ “Boys & Ladies” caps a run of five singles that marked Miss Construction’s return: “Spiel Mit Mir” in October 2025, “Back Again” in December 2025, then “Heiß,” “Hate” and “F.M.P.” through 2026. “This Is Crap” is available to pre-order now through the Out Of Line shop and on Bandcamp. About Miss Construction Miss Construction began in 2008 as a side project of Chris Pohl, who had fronted Blutengel since 1996. Pohl brought in Gordon Mocznay as co-vocalist, and the pair debuted the project at Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig that year. items.body: The Pixel Rain released “Glitching Sky” on October 2, 2026, the fourth and final advance single from the Southeast London act’s debut album, “A Sense of Danger,” due October 29 on Bandcamp, Spotify and other digital platforms. The track pushes vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Áron Siegler’s electronic side further forward, bringing futurepop and synthwave into the project’s established synthpop sound, with Siegler citing VNV Nation and Chvrches among the single’s reference points. At the center of the song is a character retreating from an unfulfilling reality into a virtual world where he can construct a more powerful version of himself. Siegler extends the idea beyond any specific technology or platform to a broader comment on how people seek distraction from anxiety, disappointment and everyday life. Siegler describes the retreat as carrying both sadness and absurdity: “The idea came from thinking about someone whose real life isn’t giving them very much, so they retreat into a virtual world where they can be whoever they want to be. There’s something quite sad about that, but also something a little ridiculous, so I wanted the story to have both sides to it. “I deliberately left the virtual world undefined because I think that kind of escape can take a lot of different forms. I’m certainly not outside of it myself. We all have things we disappear into when reality gets uncomfortable. “The music is quite fast and energetic, but the song itself takes its time building. That seemed to fit the idea: you don’t necessarily notice yourself getting drawn further and further into these little distractions until they’ve started taking up much more of your life than you intended.” The single arrives with a visualizer by Sophie Maria Vickers, built around the song’s virtual setting and digital imagery. Glitching Sky by The Pixel Rain On Bandcamp, “Glitching Sky” is bundled together with The Pixel Rain’s three earlier advance singles, “Last,” “A Sense of Danger” and “Sacrifice.” The single is also on Spotify and other major platforms. About The Pixel Rain The Pixel Rain is the solo project of vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Áron Siegler, originally from Hungary and now based in Southeast London. The project emerged from London’s underground scene with a self-titled debut EP in 2023, and mixes dark electronic and post-punk elements with guitar, electronics and industrial textures. The Pixel Rain released the first single from its forthcoming debut album, “Last,” on June 19, 2026, with a video shot in Hungary in which Siegler was joined on screen by Balázs Fűr, András Melles, Máté Breier and Máté Király-Gyeőry. The singles “A Sense of Danger” and “Sacrifice” followed over the summer, each previewing the album further. “Glitching Sky,” released October 2, 2026, is the fourth and final advance single before the debut album “A Sense of Danger” arrives on October 29, 2026. The album explores power, authority, consumerism and social unease through recurring post-apocalyptic and technological imagery.
