items.body: On 1 October 2026, Nachtmahr chose Poland to open the longest and largest tour in the project’s history: three consecutive club dates in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the opening run before IMPERIVM continues further across Europe. When Thomas Rainer and I spoke ahead of the tour, he admitted that beginning in Poland had originally been a logistical decision, but previous experience with Polish audiences made it an unexpectedly appropriate one. A new programme inevitably introduces a degree of uncertainty, and he expected the energy of the Polish crowd to remove it very quickly. Wrocław supplied a fairly emphatic confirmation. Three bands approached electronic physicality from markedly different directions, yet there was no weak transition between them. Bagger 258 worked through blunt rhythmic force, aggressive vocals and a very direct relationship with the dancefloor; Cygnosic loosened that geometry into something darker, broader and more fluid; Nachtmahr then inherited a room already fully activated and pushed it into a much less orderly state. The evening did not feel like a headliner plus obligatory support. Its construction mattered. And Wrocław really is being spoiled this autumn. The number of strong dark-electronic, industrial and gothic concerts passing through the city has reached the point where they are beginning to form a genuine season rather than a handful of unrelated bookings. This was another very persuasive addition. Bagger 258 Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil I should already have seen Bagger 258 at the NCN Warm-Up this year, but unfortunately missed them there, so Wrocław finally gave me the chance to catch up. It took very little time to understand what I had missed. The Augsburg duo, Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim “Hacke” Schmelzer, released their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” in February 2026. Its language places them firmly inside EBM: Arbeiterwut, Funktion, Kontrolle!, Werkshalle 4, “Körperkommando“, Schicht im Schacht. Machinery, work, discipline and repetitive physical action are everywhere in the imagery, while Nachtmahr themselves contributed a remix of “Werkshalle 4” to the record. Live, however, Bagger 258 were far more interesting than a catalogue of genre references might suggest. Their greatest strength was immediacy. The beats came down hard and square, the vocals had real abrasion to them, and yet the performance never became rigid. There was too much visible enjoyment onstage for that. The music was aggressive, but the aggression kept converting itself into movement. There is a considerable difference between performing the visual grammar of old-school EBM and actually making a room respond to it. Bagger 258 did the latter. The pulse was almost mechanically regular, but the communication around it was human, animated and frequently playful. They were not protecting a historical form. They were using it. For an opening band, they also did exactly what an opening band should do without ever seeming subordinate to what followed. The audience did not require a long negotiation before deciding whether it was ready to move. Bagger 258 established that physical vocabulary almost immediately, and by the end of the set the room had already shifted from people waiting for the main act into people actively participating in the evening. Rainer had told me before the tour that the right support band changes the condition in which a headliner encounters its audience. If someone else has already brought the room to a certain level, you do not have to begin from zero. Bagger 258 made the point rather convincingly. Absolute knockout. Cygnosic Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Cygnosic changed the type of pressure rather than reducing it. The Athens project of Georgios Psaroudakis has a long history within dark electro, with Psaroudakis writing, performing and producing the material himself. “Demystify”, released in 2023, was Cygnosic’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” reconstructed existing Cygnosic pieces through metal arrangements and showed how naturally heavier structures can sit inside the project’s electronic identity. That breadth could be felt live. Compared with the harder edges of Bagger 258, Cygnosic sounded more fluid and spacious, but describing it simply as “gentler” would undersell what was happening. The force had merely changed direction. Instead of striking repeatedly at the centre, the arrangements seemed to spread across the room, gathering weight through layers, melody and continuity. There was more air inside the music and more room for individual elements to develop. The rhythms still carried the performance, but the relationship between rhythm and atmosphere was different. Movement became less regimented, more continuous. The set could be forceful without constantly attacking. That made Cygnosic particularly effective in the middle position. Bagger 258 had already established the body as the evening’s main point of communication; Cygnosic kept the body engaged while changing how it moved. The result was dynamic, dark and surprisingly graceful. It also prevented the three-band bill from becoming three variations on the same impact. By the time Cygnosic finished, the audience was still physically engaged but had travelled through a noticeably different emotional texture, leaving Nachtmahr with exactly the kind of room Thomas Rainer had spoken about before the tour: warmed up, responsive and ready to be pushed considerably further. Nachtmahr Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil Photo: Karo Kratochwil When Thomas Rainer and I spoke for Side-Line in August, much of our conversation circled around a contradiction at the centre of Nachtmahr live. The project’s visual language is built from command, discipline, uniforms, hierarchy, severity and theatricalised authority. Producing that world requires enormous control: sound, lighting, costumes, movement, timing and musicianship all have to function together. Yet the result Nachtmahr seeks from the audience is almost the exact opposite. The crowd is invited to abandon restraint, surrender to rhythm and lose control inside something that has been very carefully controlled on its behalf. For Rainer, the construction starts with the songs themselves. As he told me then, “The setlist is the script for the movie we present every night on tour.” The first IMPERIVM show gave that sentence a much more concrete meaning. The album, released on 26 June 2026 through Trisol, develops methods Rainer had already begun testing on “Verboten!” rather than simply applying another layer of production to an established Nachtmahr template. In our interview, he described Verboten! not as the end point of an evolution but as the record that established the method for what followed. IMPERIVM takes that logic further while retaining the project’s unmistakable rhythmic and visual identity. Onstage, however, theory disappears very quickly behind physical action. Thomas Rainer commands a room in a way relatively few performers can. That is not simply another way of saying that he is charismatic. What impressed me was how actively he reads the response in front of him. A gesture produces a reaction; he catches that reaction and sends it back, larger. The next rhythmic hit strengthens it again. The relationship becomes circular rather than one-directional. In Wrocław, that feedback loop escalated with remarkable speed. The entire live formation is central to why it works. Nachtmahr no longer reads as one central figure surrounded by secondary decoration. There are several simultaneous points of attention across the stage, and the movement between them gives the performance much of its tension. The musicians maintain the structural discipline, while the women in the production are integral to the stage language rather than simply ornamental additions. Their choreography, posture and interaction reinforce Nachtmahr’s play with authority and submission. They contribute to the sense of order, but also to its deliberate instability. The more precisely the stage is arranged, the more excessive the activity in front of it can become. And the audience went completely wild. Not “wild” merely because people were dancing hard. What happened was cumulative. The room became denser at the front, hands were constantly raised, bodies moved forward, and the separation between active participants and passive spectators progressively disappeared. Every successful exchange with the stage seemed to authorise a larger response. That is why “madness” is both tempting and slightly inadequate as a description. The apparent madness had an architecture. It was being built. Rainer had explained in our interview that his band and crew remove much of the need for conscious control once he is onstage, allowing him to respond instinctively and become absorbed in the energy coming back from the room. He wanted the same for the audience: a framework reliable enough that people could safely lose themselves inside it. “I have a wonderful band and crew who take the need for control out of my hands, so I can completely let go onstage and simply become one with the energy of the crowd.” Wrocław demonstrated exactly what he meant. Bagger 258 and Cygnosic had already brought the audience a considerable distance. Nachtmahr did not have to spend the opening part of the set manufacturing involvement. They could begin by directing something already in motion. From there, the room became increasingly feral. One of the most striking aspects of a Nachtmahr show remains this gap between what the imagery appears to promise and what the live experience actually produces. Onstage there is hierarchy, command and discipline; in front of it, the effect is strangely collective. The imagery separates roles, while the music dissolves them. People move together. The stricter the construction onstage became, the less restrained the audience appeared. And in the middle of all that force came one of the evening’s most delicate moments. Thomas Rainer took time to remember Witek Kopytko, our colleague and a deeply valued member of the scene, who passed away earlier this year. He distributed tiny toy horses among people in the audience in Witek’s memory. It was a small, personal gesture, but precisely because nothing about it was inflated into spectacle, it carried real emotional weight. For those of us who knew Witek, worked alongside him or simply shared this scene with him over the years, the moment briefly changed the emotional temperature of the room. The concert had been built around movement, control and physical intensity; suddenly there was space for affection and remembrance. It was a genuinely beautiful tribute to a colleague who is very much missed. It also said something important about what these scenes actually consist of. Bands, promoters, journalists, photographers and audiences may occupy different roles at an event, but over years those roles begin to overlap into a community. Remembering one of its people in the middle of such a large production was not a detour from the evening. It belonged there. When the music resumed, the contrast only made the final part of the set more pronounced. The machinery returned, the crowd returned to movement, but the evening had briefly revealed something much softer underneath it. The setlist Rainer’s description of the setlist as dramaturgy becomes particularly interesting when looking at the stage sheet from Wrocław. New IMPERIVM material was not placed into an isolated promotional block; it sat among songs from different periods of Nachtmahr’s catalogue. With the clearly crossed-out alternatives on the photographed sheet omitted, the visible running order was: Wer Wind sät, Keine Lieder, Weil ich’s kann!, Liebst du mich?, Tanzdiktator, Stärker als ihr Hass, Sirenen, Heile mich, Die Straße, Kampfbereit, Beweg dich!, “Mädchen in Uniform“, Unterwerfung, Der Schlaf, Katharsis. Ending on “Katharsis” was especially fitting. By that stage, the idea had already been enacted physically for well over an hour. Wrocław, and what comes next There was something especially satisfying about watching all of this happen here. Wrocław has been remarkably well served by dark music this autumn, and the concentration of good bookings is beginning to change the rhythm of the city’s scene. It matters that international industrial, EBM, darkwave and gothic artists are not simply appearing as occasional exceptions but arriving regularly enough for audiences to develop continuity between events. That continuity is important because nights like this depend on difference as much as similarity. Bagger 258 took familiar EBM mechanics and made them feel immediate, aggressive and highly physical rather than nostalgic. Cygnosic widened that physicality into something more fluid, melodic and atmospheric. Nachtmahr then absorbed everything accumulated during the previous sets and used it as raw material for a performance based on reciprocal escalation. The Polish IMPERIVM opening continues with Poznań at Pod Minogą on 2 October and Warsaw at VooDoo Club on 3 October, before the tour moves on internationally. Their debut album “Aufwärts gehts bergab” was released in February 2026 and includes remixes by Nachtmahr, NordarR and Menticide; Side-Line covered the album in a March 2024 interview with the duo. Cygnosic is the Athens-based dark-electro project of Georgios Psaroudakis. “Demystify” appeared in 2023 as the project’s seventh full-length album, while 2025’s “Theorem” revisited Cygnosic compositions through metal arrangements without abandoning the project’s electronic core. Side-Line first covered the Nachtmahr connection in 2019, when Cygnosic toured with Nachtmahr and labelmates C-lekktor behind the “Epiphany” LP. Nachtmahr, founded by Austrian musician Thomas Rainer in 2007, has developed a distinctive language around hard electronic rhythm, theatrical authority, confrontation, discipline and increasingly broad stylistic freedom. IMPERIVM is the latest stage of that development, while the current tour is the largest and longest undertaken under the Nachtmahr name. The Wrocław opening showed how carefully the three-band construction worked: Bagger 258 established the body, Cygnosic changed the way it moved, and Nachtmahr took control of what had already been set in motion. By the end, the contradiction Thomas Rainer and I had discussed before the tour, extreme control on one side of the stage and deliberate surrender on the other, no longer needed explaining. It was visible everywhere in the room.

items.body: Town And Towers Records has signed Swiss duo CØLDSTAR, releasing the band’s new single “Last Night On Earth” on 2 October 2026. The track is the Bern-based darkwave, synthpop and coldwave act’s first release on the Danish label. “Last Night On Earth” follows a narrator watching Earth’s final hours from roughly seven hundred miles above the planet, aboard a spacecraft where the oxygen cycles mechanically and the view of the dying world shrinks to a reflection in glass. The lyrics state the moment directly: “The blue marble fades in a rear view of glass / I watch from the silence as centuries pass.” There is no rescue attempt in the story and no final message, only “a velvet curtain, and we’re not coming back.” Dark synth layers, pulsing electronic rhythms and melancholic melodies carry the track’s icy, futuristic atmosphere. Town And Towers names VNV Nation and Black Nail Cabaret as reference points for that sound. Recommend to fans of Solar Fake, Final Selection, Depeche Mode, Covenant and The Soft Moon. CØLDSTAR’s ‘Last Night On Earth’ is the duo’s first release for Town And Towers Records “Last Night On Earth” is out now as a digital single, also streaming via Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, SoundCloud and Tidal. Last Night On Earth by CØLDSTAR Town And Towers Records’ recent roster also includes deZeption, signed in 2024, and Hatif, whose album “Small States” arrived via the label in 2025. About CØLDSTAR Martin Baumann and Michael Freund record as CØLDSTAR from Bern, Switzerland, mixing darkwave, synthpop, coldwave and retro-futurist synth sounds. The duo’s songs use space and science-fiction imagery to address isolation, memory, technology, longing and human existence. CØLDSTAR’s early releases included a 2021 cover of Nine Inch Nails‘ “Hurt.” The band built out its own catalogue with the “Coming Home” EP in 2023, then the debut album “CØSMIC DUST” in 2024 via Swiss Dark Nights, combining atmospheric electronics, synthpop melody and darker post-punk influences. Singles “Time Machine,” “Astronaut’s Lament,” “Last Dance” and “Post-Punk Robot” followed. “Post-Punk Robot” reached number 2 on the Deutsche Alternative Charts in 2026. “Last Night On Earth” is the fifth single CØLDSTAR has issued since “CØSMIC DUST,” and the first through Town And Towers Records.

items.body: Danish/UK electronic duo Oui Plastique release the single “For The Cry Of Anguish” on October 16, 2026 through Town and Towers Records. It is the fourth and final single from the project’s second album, “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It”, due November 27, 2026 on the same Danish label. A Bandcamp page for the single had not gone live at the time of writing. Oui Plastique close the singles campaign for ‘Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It’ “For The Cry Of Anguish” follows three earlier singles from the same album: “Revival” in April 2026, “Linger” on June 12, 2026, and “Spirit” on September 4, 2026. “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It” is Oui Plastique’s second album, following the 2022 debut “Fraternity of Strangers”. It runs 14 tracks and releases digitally, on CD and on vinyl through Town and Towers Records on November 27, 2026. Oui Plastique set up the song’s premise directly: “For The Cry Of Anguish is a song about seeing something you were never meant to see – and discovering that some things, once witnessed, can never be unseen.“ Oui Plastique previously posted a teaser video for “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It” to the duo’s YouTube channel, titled “Oui Plastique – ‘Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It’ – Album Teaser”. About Oui Plastique Oui Plastique is the duo of Martin Nyrup (Denmark) and James Thomas (UK). The project grew out of a 2017 collaboration between Nyrup, also one half of the dark wave duo Perpacity, and Thomas, of the band DVL, who together recorded the album “Convergence” that year. In 2018 the pair recorded a three-track covers EP for the UnMute project, a tribute to Mute Records, released on Bandcamp as “UM EP 04” on February 1, 2019. Before the debut album, four of its eventual tracks appeared as standalone digital singles: “Failure” on March 8, 2021, “The Fear” on May 28, 2021, “Crossing Over” on September 24, 2021, and “Wish Yourself Away” on November 26, 2021. The 11-track debut album “Fraternity of Strangers” followed on January 28, 2022, on CD through ScentAir Records. A remastered edition of “Convergence” followed in 2022. In August 2025, the UnMute covers were remastered and reissued across platforms as the EP “UnMute”, featuring the Martin Gore-associated tracks “Compulsion”, “The Bottom Line” and “It Doesn’t Matter Two”, through Town and Towers Records. Nyrup’s other project, Perpacity, released the album “Discordia” in 2023 and the Danish-language single “Lille Flamme” in May 2025. “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It” arrives on November 27, 2026. It is Oui Plastique’s first full-length through Town and Towers Records, following the 2022 debut on ScentAir Records.

About Death Strip Death Strip pairs Jonas Moberg, a Swedish producer and drummer based on Gotland, with vocalist Culture Yob, also known as Son of Daughter, based in Hastings, England. Moberg played drums in the Swedish rock band Jumper, which released three albums and eleven singles between 1996 and 2000, and later played live drums for Paloma Faith early in her career. Culture Yob co-founded the band Gobsausage with Takalina and Miss Halski in the early 2000s, and also co-founded Charles of London, according to the band. The two met in the 2000s and lived in neighboring warehouse flats in Shoreditch, London, where they shared a goods lift. They now live apart, Moberg on Gotland and Culture Yob in Hastings, and write and record Death Strip’s music remotely. The two have never been in the same room for a Death Strip session. “Flash Back,” released October 8, 2026, is the fourth single Death Strip has made this way.

items.body: Chicago industrial dance band My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult released “The Reincarnation of Luna” on 2 October 2001 through SleazeBox Records, the band’s own label, distributed by Invisible Records. The album turns 25 this year. My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult recorded and mixed the album at Starlust Studios in Los Angeles, with Buzz McCoy producing. Groovie Mann and Buzz McCoy wrote all twelve tracks, performed with the Bomb Gang Girlz, and Chris Greene handled mastering. The tracklist runs: “Radio Silicon” “The Untouchable Class” “Hour of Zero” “The Kult Konnection” “Girl Without a Planet” “Temptation Serenade” “Bettie” “Flesh Playhouse” “Heelz Afire” “Jungle of Love” “Asylum Disciple” “Theme De Luna” “The Reincarnation of Luna” was My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult’s first release on their own SleazeBox Records imprint, following “A Crime for All Seasons” (1997) on Red Ant Records. The band released a companion remix set, “Golden Pillz: The Luna Remixes,” and a live album, “Elektrik Inferno,” in the same period. In 2007, the band re-recorded and remixed the album for Rykodisc under the title “The Resurrection of Luna,” adding “Ocean of Hate,” “Hallowed Be My Name” and a remix of “Temptation Serenade.” The original 2001 version remains available through the band’s own site. About My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult, often shortened to Thrill Kill Kult or TKK, formed in Chicago in 1987. Groovie Mann (born Frankie Nardiello) and Buzz McCoy (born Marston Daley) met that year while touring with Ministry and began recording music for an unfinished art film of the same name. Wax Trax! Records released the completed songs as a three-track EP, and when it sold well, the full-length “I See Good Spirits and I See Bad Spirits” followed in 1988. “Confessions of a Knife…” (1990) became one of Wax Trax!’s best-selling releases, and “Sexplosion!” (1991) pushed the band toward a more psychedelic house and disco sound while drawing attention from Interscope Records, which signed the band and released the alternative-radio single “Sex on Wheelz.” “13 Above the Night” (1993) and “Hit & Run Holiday” (1995) followed on Interscope before the band parted ways with the label in 1996. “A Crime for All Seasons” (1997) came out on Red Ant Records, and “The Reincarnation of Luna” (2001) marked the start of the band’s own SleazeBox Records imprint, distributed by Invisible Records. Rykodisc later became the band’s home, reissuing its back catalog alongside the rarities set “Dirty Little Secrets,” the mash-up album “Diamonds & Daggerz” (2004) and the long-shelved “Gay, Black and Married” (2005). SleazeBox partnered with Italy’s Rustblade label in 2009, issuing “Blood + Dope + Sin + Gold” (2008), “Death Threat” (2009) and “Sinister Whisperz” (2011), and Side-Line covered the band’s 2020 “Sinister Whisperz” retrospective installment, “The Rykodisc Years.” Buzz McCoy has also remixed tracks for KMFDM, Pigface and other acts, and recorded as Excessive Force with KMFDM’s Sascha Konietzko. The band has contributed songs to film soundtracks including “Cool World” (1992), “The Crow” (1994), in which members also appeared performing in a nightclub scene, “The Flintstones” (1994), “Showgirls” (1995) and “Baseketball” (1998). My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult toured the US in spring 2026 with support from Heavy Halo, as Side-Line reported at the time, continuing to perform a catalog that this October marks the 25th anniversary of “The Reincarnation of Luna.”

items.body: Swedish synthpop act Split Vision release the single “Cold War” on 2 October 2026 through the Danish label Town And Towers Records. The track is the second single from the band’s upcoming album “BetaCity”, due on 6 November 2026 on streaming, CD and vinyl. “Cold War” follows “Out of Nowhere”, released on 10 September 2026 as the first single from “BetaCity.” The new track moves into darker territory than its predecessor. Sequenced synthesizers underpin lyrics that revisit Cold War-era paranoia, isolation and secrecy as a metaphor for conflict and uncertainty. The lyrics were written by the band’s label manager, Stig Wintendorff, in the 1980s. The chorus repeats the song’s central image: “Dancing in the shadows of the Cold War night.” The single’s cover artwork draws on Cold War-era imagery: masks, military hardware and Soviet-style visual motifs. Split Vision’s ‘BetaCity’ album Split Vision’s previous album, “Echoes of a New Spell” (2025, Town And Towers Records), drew on the synthesizers and recording approach associated with early Depeche Mode. “BetaCity” turns instead toward the early sound of Alphaville. Town And Towers Records describes the album’s sound as combining “warm analogue synthesizers with colder digital textures, wavetable sounds, sequenced bass lines and atmospheric pads.” Recommended for fans of Alphaville, Depeche Mode and Erasure. About Split Vision Split Vision formed in Sweden in 1985, when two teenage friends started writing synthpop with influences from Depeche Mode, Yazoo, Erasure and Pet Shop Boys. Two more members joined, and the four-piece played discotheques in North Eastern Skåne and appeared on regional radio and talent shows through the late 1980s. Platinum Records released the single “How Will I Ever” in 1988, and “So Many Times” became a minor hit in Sweden before the group disbanded. Dan Hansson and Henric Palmqvist, two of the original members, restarted Split Vision in the spring of 2019 to write new material rooted in the band’s 1980s sound. “We wanted to take the audience on a journey back to carefully carved arpeggios, that smell of Moog and Yamaha DX-7,” the band said of that return, describing music with “strong melodies performed by a distinct lead and backed by a contemporary vocoder.” The result, “Among the Stars,” arrived on 1 October 2020, with lyrics and soundscapes that reference the cosmos. Split Vision signed to the Scandinavian label Town And Towers Records in 2022 and has released several singles and EPs since. A music video for “Lust,” directed by Norwegian filmmaker Öystein Thorsen, followed in August 2024 and won awards at the New York Tri-State International Film Festival and the KHIFF Krimson Horyzon International Film Festival in India. The band has also toured as a support act for the British group China Crisis. “Echoes of a New Spell” followed in 2025, and “Out of Nowhere” opened the “BetaCity” campaign on 10 September 2026. “Cold War,” released 2 October 2026, is the second single from that album, due on 6 November 2026 through Town And Towers Records.

items.body: This album from the Danish project Black Vault was actually released quite some time ago—back in the spring of 2025. With the telling title “Death Obsessed”, we are presented with five tracks. There is no room for fun in this sonic universe; instead, we are confronted with a dark, nihilistic-sounding whole. The atmosphere is carefully constructed and accentuated by occasional spoken-word samples, creating a tormented listening experience. Blending elements of Dark-Ambient, Industrial, Noise, and even Ritual music, the production is sometimes a tiny chaotic yet undeniably well-crafted. The combination of influences is fascinating, and, to my mind, the opening two tracks are particularly compelling. Black Vault transports us into an illusory world of ruin. The only thing missing, for me, is an absolute climax—though that certainly doesn’t mean this isn’t a great record. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission”: The Hollow Sighs Of Putrid Emission by Black Vault About Black Vault Black Vault is a Danish project working in occult industrial and death-industrial territory on the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen. The project’s debut album, “Hymns To The Great Devourer”, was released on Dunkelheit Produktionen in 2023. “Death Obsessed” is the follow-up, recorded between 2023 and 2024 and released on March 1, 2025, mixed and mastered by Grant Richardson at Hex Audio Labs.

The five-track digital release moves the project’s minimal electro sound into more dynamic techno territory. Elements EP by CUBIC ‘Elements’ draws on 80s electro, 90s techno and dub techno “Elements” draws on 1980s electro, 1990s techno in the style of R&S Records, and acid and dub techno, the reference points that have run through Cubic’s sound over the years, with Alfa Matrix noting a nod toward contemporary acts such as Bicep and Modeselektor. Opening track “Future Past” and the two versions of “BangBang,” a Detroit edit and a Chicago edit, push the EP toward a more dancefloor-oriented, energetic direction. “A Fish” and “Chord Memory” keep the minimal sequences, vintage electronics and repeating patterns that recur through Cubic’s releases. ‘Elements’ EP tracklist “Future Past” (4:31) “BangBang” (Detroit edit) (4:26) “A Fish” (4:35) “Chord Memory” (4:55) “BangBang” (Chicago edit) (4:10) The EP is a digital release, available as a download via the Alfa Matrix Bandcamp page, with streaming included, at up to 24-bit/44.1kHz. About Cubic Cubic is the electronic project of Belgian artist Franky Deblomme, also known for his earlier work as 808 Dot Pop. Deblomme signed Cubic to Alfa Matrix and released the project’s label debut EP, “Alphabet Hymn,” on March 9, 2021. The five-track EP combined vintage Dusseldorf synth influences, Berlin techno, 1990s Manchester rave and EBM, built entirely on hardware synthesizers and effects at Deblomme’s Bong 13 studio, and included a remix by label mates 808 Dot Pop. Later that month, Cubic reworked an earlier 808 Dot Pop album into “The Cubic Temperature,” released March 26, 2021 with an exclusive Bandcamp megamix bonus track. Cubic’s debut album, “The Cubic Alphabet,” arrived on June 18, 2021. The project continued with the EP “Phonic Lessons Part 3” on December 7, 2021, then the singles “Exit – Frankfurt” on April 7, 2022 and the four-track “Exit – Ghent” on June 29, 2022, each tied to a specific city’s electronic scene. The EPs “c64” (September 18, 2023) and “c128” (December 6, 2023), both referencing Commodore home computers, preceded the album “Back To Basic,” released on Alfa Matrix on June 4, 2024 with a Kraftwerk-indebted sound made using the first Belgian-made drum computer (Modor DR2) and synthesizer (Modor NF1). Cubic released the vinyl EP “EFM01 (Black)” in an ultra-limited run in June 2025, then the digital EP “EFM02” in October 2025 and the rework album “Back To 808” in December 2025. The twin EPs “CB-708” and “CB-128,” revisiting “Back To 808,” came out in February 2026. “Elements,” out October 2, 2026, is Cubic’s newest EP on Alfa Matrix. The EP extends the single into an eight-track release. “Information Systems” opens the record with a long-form soundscape built entirely from spoken samples about the mythology of computing. “The Insider” addresses privileged knowledge and how much of what people take as fact is actually interpretation or assumption. “Pills (in f sharp)” reworks the album track “Pills” into a different key, turning its “I want more pills” refrain into both a chant and a comment on the pursuit of quick fixes. “Underneath The Neon Lights” also appears on the EP. Three remixes of the title track close the release. New York act Crash Course In Science turns the song into a club-oriented dance track. People Theatre take it in a more melodic direction before a detuned lead takes over. items.body: Antonio Vivaldi, the red-haired priest and virtuoso violinist, spent much of his career as music master at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian orphanage famous for its music. He composed The Four Seasons around 1720, while serving as court chapel master in Mantua. In 1725 they were published in Amsterdam as the opening concertos of his Op. 8, a set of twelve titled Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione. After Vivaldi’s death in 1741 his music was largely forgotten for nearly two centuries, and the Seasons returned with the revival of his work in the twentieth century. Each concerto follows the same plan of three movements, fast, slow and fast, for solo violin, strings and continuo. Each was also printed with a sonnet, and Vivaldi set its images in the music: birdsong, a summer storm, peasants dancing at the harvest, teeth chattering in the winter cold. Few works have been recorded more often, and the versions range from full modern string orchestras to small groups with one player on each part, on modern or period instruments. Nigel Kennedy’s 1989 album alone sold millions of copies and brought the music to a huge new audience. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the 10 best recordings of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. Giuliano Carmignola, Venice Baroque Orchestra, Andrea Marcon Giuliano Carmignola’s 1999 recording with Andrea Marcon and the Venice Baroque Orchestra is the natural first choice. Carmignola takes the fast movements at high speed and with great energy, yet the textures stay light and the playing crisp. The tension mounts steadily through each concerto, and Winter is especially gripping. At times the pace is pushed almost too far, but the excitement more than makes up for it. The disc also includes three other Vivaldi violin concertos, recorded here for the first time. Carmignola Amazon Presto Apple Fabio Biondi, Europa Galante Fabio Biondi and Europa Galante first recorded the Seasons in 1991, in a celebrated version. Nine years later they returned to the work, once more playing from Vivaldi’s manuscripts rather than the printed edition. Compared with Carmignola, the performance is freer and less predictable. Biondi’s bowing is full of surprises, the bass lines are attacked almost like percussion, and the storm that ends Summer is fierce and very fast. The slow movements, in contrast, are tender and deeply felt. Not everyone will enjoy its liberties, but it is one of the most imaginative recordings of the work. Biondi Amazon Presto Apple Rachel Podger, Brecon Baroque Rachel Podger’s 2017 recording with Brecon Baroque uses just one player on each part, which turns the Seasons into chamber music. Even so, the sound is full rather than thin, helped by an excellent recording. Podger plays with easy brilliance and obvious pleasure, and the rest of the group is just as lively. The birdsong in the first movement of Spring is especially vivid. For all its small scale, this is not a radical reading: it stays closer to tradition than some other recent versions. Podger Amazon Presto Apple Nigel Kennedy, English Chamber Orchestra This 1989 album owed much of its huge success to Nigel Kennedy’s personality. He directs the English Chamber Orchestra himself, and the recording places his violin firmly in the foreground. Kennedy adds his own ornaments and treats the tempo freely, yet the playing remains disciplined. The heavy vibrato is a matter of taste, and from Autumn onward a few added effects sound odd. Even so, the performance is as lively as ever. Kennedy Amazon Presto Apple Adrian Chandler, La Serenissima This 2015 recording with La Serenissima is the first of Adrian Chandler’s two versions of the work. Like Biondi, he worked from Vivaldi’s manuscript parts and prepared his own edition, but the result is very different. Chandler lets the sonnets guide the performance, and his phrasing often recalls folk song. The rhythms are taut, the textures transparent, and he adds very few ornaments of his own. The biggest surprise comes at the very start of Autumn, where a Baroque guitar joins the accompaniment and the familiar opening tune is phrased in an unexpected way. The disc also includes two bassoon concertos with Peter Whelan. For anyone who thinks they know the Seasons too well, this is the recording to hear. Chandler Amazon Presto Apple Simon Standage, The English Concert, Trevor Pinnock Trevor Pinnock’s 1981 recording with the English Concert was one of the early period-instrument versions, and it has aged well. Pinnock directs from the harpsichord, and Simon Standage plays the solo part with confidence and bite. The ensemble sound is warm and full, but never heavy. The performance avoids sudden shocks and extremes, so it can seem a little plain compared with the bolder recordings that came later. In return, it offers a balanced and deeply satisfying account of all four concertos. Pinnock Amazon Presto Apple Nils-Erik Sparf, Drottningholm Baroque Ensemble The Drottningholm Baroque Ensemble’s 1984 recording, led from the violin by Nils-Erik Sparf, is understated by design, and that is its charm. Sparf shapes the phrases with subtle changes of speed and volume, and he never hurries. In the accompaniment, a pipe organ is often heard prominently instead of the more common harpsichord, which gives the performance a softer edge. The tuning is excellent, the tone rounder than usual for period instruments, and the players sound as if they enjoy every moment. Those who want high drama should look elsewhere, but this is a recording to come back to. Sparf Amazon Presto Apple Felix Ayo, I Musici I Musici’s 1959 recording with Felix Ayo was a best seller long before period instruments changed how this music is performed, and its elegance has not dated. The players work without a conductor and move as one, and Ayo’s solos are full of feeling, his virtuosity never put on show for its own sake. The scenes in the sonnets are painted with care: in the slow movement of Spring, the barking of the goatherd’s dog, played by the viola, comes through clearly. The vibrato is moderate and the tempos are generally relaxed. It remains one of the most rewarding of the traditional versions. Ayo Amazon Presto Apple Itzhak Perlman, London Philharmonic Orchestra Where Ayo is restrained, Itzhak Perlman’s 1976 recording with the London Philharmonic is unashamedly lavish: a full string orchestra, a sweet tone and a soloist in the grand manner. The slow movements are the heart of the recording, with Perlman shaping each melody in long, unbroken lines. Next to the smaller groups, it can feel heavy, and the fast movements have less bite. For listeners who care more about beauty of sound than period style, it remains a strong old-school choice. Perlman Amazon Presto Apple Janine Jansen As in Podger’s version, Janine Jansen’s 2004 recording uses just one player on each part, but here the instruments are modern. Her small group, which includes her brother on cello and her father at the keyboard, plays with clean textures and plenty of vigor. Jansen is at her finest in the quiet music, where her playing has a rare delicacy. Some accents are overstated, and the tempos are on the safe side. The disc is also short, with nothing but the four concertos in under forty minutes, but it is a performance with a character of its own. items.body: Once a song reaches the stage, its authors have to negotiate with a whole new set of circumstances: the room, the volume, the audience, and whatever mood everyone brought through the door. For Brooklyn alternative rock outfit The Amatory Murder, that unpredictability is part of the appeal. Their new live album, We’ve Lost Our Minds: The Amatory Murder Live, is out today, October 2, bringing twelve performances from Brooklyn’s Lucky 13 Saloon to streaming platforms. Drawing on songs from across their catalog, the album documents the heavier, more spontaneous side of a group whose music brings together alternative rock, classic rock, and electronics. The familiar melodies and arrangements remain central, while the live setting gives the material room to change its disposition. For a band that has spent years building its audience through club shows, festivals, and independent touring across the United States, these recordings offer a document of the work done face to face. “There’s something that happens to these songs when we play them live that you can’t completely recreate in the studio,” says Xian Murder. “The energy changes, and sometimes the songs become something different altogether. We wanted to capture that honestly.” Vocalist, songwriter, producer, and founder Xian Murder leads the band alongside bassist Binx Noir and guitarist Jake Haimowitz. Their influences stretch from the expansive rock of Pink Floyd and Muse to Nine Inch Nails, Depeche Mode, The Cult, Joy Division, and David Bowie, a range that helps account for the combination of heavy guitars, electronic detail, and melodic songwriting at the center of their music. Alex Reyes recorded the album at Lucky 13 Saloon, with Dan Kramer handling the mix at Brooklyn’s Skillman Labs and Mark Allen Miller mastering. The release turns that local stage into a meeting point for listeners further afield, giving longtime followers another perspective on the songs and newcomers a way into the band’s live repertoire. We’ve Lost Our Minds is available now on Spotify, Apple Music, and other major streaming platforms. Watch below: Later this month, The Amatory Murder return to Lucky 13 Saloon for a Halloween Eve show with Witchforce, Mykey Massacre, and Mannequin Heist. It is a fitting place to pick up where the recording leaves off, with another evening in the room that gave the album its setting. October 30 — Brooklyn, NY — Lucky 13 Saloon, 644 Sackett Street, with Witchforce, Mykey Massacre, and Mannequin Heist. Ages 21+. items.body: A Faustian bargain begins with the ancient human suspicion that the universe can be persuaded to overlook consequence. We trade tomorrow for today, permanence for appetite, conscience for advantage, imagining that the account will somehow remain unsettled. Yet nature keeps exquisite books. Every shortcut alters the road; every borrowed fire casts its own darkness. The tragedy is seldom that we receive nothing for the price. Quite often, we receive precisely what we asked for. Power, knowledge, youth, wealth: these may all arrive intact. The horror lies in discovering, only afterward, that possession and fulfillment were never the same thing. Las Vegas has always been a fitting place for bad bargains. Money changes hands beneath artificial stars, luck is treated as a temporary religion, and every promise of sudden fortune carries an unspoken question about what somebody might surrender to obtain it. In the video for And It Was Night’s The Fever, composer and sound designer Rani Sharone turns that temptation into a compact morality play, casting himself as both gambler and Devil while an obsession gradually takes possession of the room. Inspired by the Twilight Zone episode of the same name, The Fever takes the old Faustian bargain and filters it through addiction. Sharone’s gambler appears trapped between appetite and consequence, surrounded by projected animation, theatrical props, and backgrounds that continually push the setting away from ordinary reality. The imagery works particularly well with the song’s dark electro-pop foundation, where Depeche Mode, Danny Elfman, The Cure, and Nick Cave provide useful coordinates without swallowing Sharone’s own identity. He calls the result “Dark Noir Pop,” an apt description for music that feels equally suited to a nightclub, a crooked casino, and the closing credits of some lost supernatural thriller. The Devil, naturally, has the easier job. Temptation requires charm before punishment enters the picture, and Sharone plays both sides of that transaction with an appropriately theatrical touch. By reducing the production to two characters embodied by one performer, the video turns its budgetary limitations into part of its psychological logic. Gambler and tempter begin to resemble two expressions of the same compulsion. “I didn’t want to do a literal retelling of the Twilight Zone episode the song was based off of,” says Sharone. “For practical reasons and budgetary/production limitations I chose to create something that I could pull off with a very limited crew and budget. The result ended up being me playing both characters, the gambler and devil, and shooting in front of custom commissioned animated projections to set the stage with props to make it as theatrical as I could to sell the story. I used a couple iconic horror sources to direct and inspire my visual FX supervisor when creating the background designs. Namely from The Shining. which inspired the look of the hotel room the gambler is in, and a couple visual cues from Creepshow for the more surreal background designs. Those with a keen eye will recognize them.” Watch the video for The Fever below: That horror lineage suits Sharone, whose résumé ranges from Puscifer and Stolen Babies to orchestral work performed by Hilary Hahn and recent contributions to the music team behind K-Pop Demon Hunters. With The Fever, his return to writing his own songs feels especially pointed: desire becomes addiction, luck becomes captivity, and the Devil barely needs to cheat. The gambler has already brought his weakness to the table. Sharone’s casino nightmare will also find an audience in Los Angeles tonight, Friday, October 2, when The Fever screens at El Cid as part of a monthly screening with a suitably spooky selection. Doors open at 7 p.m., with the screening beginning at 8 p.m.—another opportunity to watch the gambler discover exactly how much his good fortune costs. items.body: Winter Sect have discovered one of goth’s better-kept secrets: graveyards can be funny places. Not funny in the sitcom sense, unless your sitcom happens to involve velvet sleeves, low fog, marble angels, and a bass player turning cemetery dirt into a dance floor, but funny in the grand old rock-and-roll sense that the concept of memento mori has always looked a little less terrifying once somebody places a wreath of backbeat on the coffin. Made up of Sister Ex alumna Claudia Neuman on bass and vocals, guitarist Anthony Piazza, keyboardist and vocalist Heather Wayward, and drummer Darryl J. Dardenne, the DC/Baltimore group have previously favored the colder end of Gothic psychedelia and glam rock. Graveyard Girl, however, loosens the corset. Funk, garage rock, indie pop and even bossa nova slip into the bloodstream, bringing a loose, easy groove beneath the song’s ’60s pop whimsy while the band keeps one boot planted firmly in post-punk soil. Neuman’s bass is responsible for the initial crime, strutting around with the casual confidence of someone who has found the liquor cabinet during a wake. Wayward’s keyboards add splashes of color around Piazza’s guitar, while Dardenne keeps the song moving with a lightness that gives its cemetery imagery room to grin. The melody has the cheeky charm of a vintage pop single, its tuneful bounce making the invitation to wander among the graves sound suspiciously like a proposition for a Sunday afternoon date. Siouxsie and the Banshees, March Violets, Strange Boutique and more hover somewhere in the family tree, although Winter Sect sound especially amused by the possibilities of their own material here. According to Wayward, that playful turn happened almost accidentally during rehearsal: “The song pretty much started with Claudia grooving out on a bass line,” she says. “It was catchy and I thought let’s do something completely different and not so serious and macabre. First the hook was discovered and we built from there. So with that funk of a groove my mind started walking. Where? Through the graveyard of course. It came together in a cool way and a little twist at the end just makes it fun.” That sense of fun carries into the video, which sends the band wandering through the necropolis in slow motion among candles, veils and fog. Somebody communes with the departed, everybody looks appropriately dressed for the occasion, and the solemn machinery of Gothic imagery gains a sly little wink. You half expect one of the headstones to start keeping time. Watch the video for Graveyard Girl below: Winter Sect began in late 2023 when California native Neuman and Piazza formed the project around feedback-heavy goth, New Wave, industrial and psychedelic influences. Mystic Twin and Haunted House followed in 2024, with Say Goodbye appearing in 2026. Graveyard Girl, taken from the forthcoming EP Offering, suggests Winter Sect have figured out that darkness becomes far more interesting when somebody remembers to leave room for mischief and a tune you can hum on the way home. items.body: An ache moves forward He steps back I step forward It all turns black He steps forward I step back Some relationships develop their own terrible choreography: one person advances, the other retreats, and a moment of contact sends both back through the same steps. On Annihilate, underground post-industrial producer and vocalist Lana Del Rabies gives that exhausted dance a setting of metallic percussion, dissonant strings, and voices that seem to drift through the walls. The prospect of closeness carries a threat of disappearance, as though reaching for another person might cost you the outline of yourself. Released through her own Feral Crone Recordings, the single revisits the gothic industrial territory of her 2023 album STREGA BEATA. Among her most accessible recordings to date, Annihilate brings its melody into clearer view within a dense, unsettling arrangement, with echoes of mid-career Nine Inch Nails, early Chelsea Wolfe, Dead Can Dance, and Godflesh. Written and produced by Lana Del Rabies, the track features bass, guitar, and additional instrumentation from Zach Wise, formerly of experimental black metal band Hissing. Deeply reverberant string tones open the song, their discord setting the room askew before a soft metallic beat begins carrying it forward. Creaking noises punctuate the haze, while thudding distortion stays buried beneath the mix, suggesting a heartbeat accelerating at the approach of something unwelcome. Her singing is soft, breathy, and eerily close; farther away, wails stretch across the recording like cries attempting to reach the living. The whole thing suggests a deserted Victorian factory, its decaying rooms still occupied by machinery and something considerably harder to identify. That dusty, corroded atmosphere recalls the gothic industrial aesthetics of the 1990s, with every small sound acquiring an uncomfortable physical presence. The lyrics begin with images converging in reverse and a moment suspended in time. From there, the exchange becomes a sequence of opposing movements: his withdrawal prompts her advance, his approach sends her backward. “Push pull fade” reduces the relationship to its recurring mechanism. Hearing her name briefly promises recognition, but the next attempt at contact leaves her grasping in vain. By the time the title enters the refrain, desire reads as a force capable of wearing away the person who feels it. Directed and edited by Lana Del Rabies/Sam An, the video translates that instability into grainy woodland footage, overlapping figures, and close-ups that dissolve before they can offer much certainty. Pale dresses and fabric catch the light against dense foliage; raised arms, blurred faces, and bodies close to the ground recur through successive layers of exposure. Black-and-white images give way to smeared color, turning the setting into something resembling a damaged reel of folk horror. The footage was shot by Jane Slater, whose video credits include Dildox, Brood Faye, and Sacred Skin, and Vox Porter of Sleek Teeth. Watch the video for Annihilate below: Lana Del Rabies began with early experiments sampling female pop musicians into noise tracks, a practice reflected in the project’s name. An has since developed a body of work spanning industrial music, gothic electronics, and experimental heaviness, examining human brutality and the prospect of apocalypse. Her recordings have earned attention from The Quietus, Metal Hammer, and Anthony Fantano, while her live performances have taken her to festivals including Roadburn, Coldwaves, Sled Island, Prepare the Ground, Northwest Terror Fest, and Soulcrusher. She has toured with Author & Punisher, 3TEETH, Pharmakon, JPEGMAFIA, and John Wiese, and opened shows for artists including clipping., Midwife, HEALTH, and Bell Witch. In 2025, An founded the art-focused label Feral Crone Recordings and released Le Temps Viendra and Omnipotent Fuck. She is currently working on a studio record with former members of Hissing, due in 2027. Listen to Annihilate below and order the single here. items.body: Dreams may be among the strangest territories available to us. Each night, the mind constructs worlds without asking permission from physics, geography, biography, or common sense. We meet people who never existed, return to places that vanished years ago, fall in love with strangers, lose ourselves, recover ourselves, and wake carrying the emotional residue of events that never occurred. There is something almost miraculous in this private universe, because within it we are briefly released from the limits imposed by circumstance. Thought offers a similar freedom. We can imagine nearly anything, even when reality permits us to accomplish only a fraction of it. For Venus Volcanism, the Iceland-based project of Crete-born vocalist, musician, and producer Rena Rasouli, dreams become both refuge and research subject. Her new song, “Dreams,” inhabits the uncertain region between waking life and the private worlds that continue behind our eyes. Rasouli created the song exactly one year ago as the first snow settled across the peaks surrounding Siglufjörður, Iceland’s northernmost town. She keeps a journal beside her bed, recording complete dreams when possible and preserving stray images when that is all sleep leaves behind. Before sleeping, she gives herself a small invocation: “As I close my eyelids and sleep takes me, gently or not, please show me something that will help me understand myself a little better.” Dreams drifts somewhere between dark pop, ambient composition, experimental electronics, and neoclassical music, with affinities to This Mortal Coil, Julee Cruise, Penelope Trappes, and Zola Jesus. Rasouli’s voice occupies the center while drones, synthesizers, arpeggiated figures, and suspended textures create an unstable sense of location. Beauty and unease coexist. The song seems to hover between desire imagined and desire remembered. Its love story belongs to an imaginary lover, though imagination hardly makes the emotion less consequential. Desperation, longing, idealization, and obsession can become perfectly real experiences even when their object remains beyond reach. “Have you ever found yourself dreaming with your eyes open? I honestly don’t know how many times I have done it while diving into Icelandic pools,” says Rasouli. “Especially during winter, I feel like I am balancing somewhere between the conscious and the unconscious, and sometimes I don’t even know how the day has passed. I am and I am not. I exist and I do not exist. I do everything I am supposed to do; I move through the day as I should, but if you know me well enough, you might see it in my eyes: I am somewhere in between.” This suspended condition also governs the video, directed by Tassos Gkoletsos with help from friends and members of the Siglufjörður community. Northern Iceland’s long winter darkness turns ordinary routines into strange repetitions: tending plants, bathing, working, exercising, moving through familiar rooms while another existence unfolds internally. “During those months, I always find myself somewhere in between,” Rasouli continues. “I do everything I need to do and I’m relatively functional, but everything feels like autopilot. At the same time, another scene is taking place inside my head. I dream and imagine other things while going through the ordinary routines of everyday life, like watering my plants, having my bath, working, and going to the gym.” Perhaps this is why Dreams feels so intimate. Rasouli treats imagination as a parallel dimension of daily existence, one without measurable coordinates yet capable of altering everything that happens after we return. items.body: Lift the veil, see what I’ve become An exoskeletal pantheon Born again from bone and breath To spread the living gospel of death On Tears for the Dying‘s blistering new gothic track Devour Me, Adria Stembridge drags the band back toward its earlier roots with a slower, heavier gait, then breaks that crawl apart with abrupt tempo changes that make the song feel unstable beneath your feet. Stembridge handles drum machine, guitar, bass, and vocals, building the track from dark guitar figures, blunt low-end pressure, and drums that move with the patience of something following you home. Her vocals hang above it all in a cold echo, less concerned with theatrical grandstanding than with letting the words rot in the air for a second before the next image lands. You can hear Bauhaus in the skeletal guitar work, Alien Sex Fiend in the queasy theatricality, and PiL and Fields of the Nephilim in the sense that somebody has wandered far enough from civilization to start inventing a religion. That religious impulse becomes central once the lyrics start opening the trapdoor. Stembridge draws from cosmic horror, but the terror here feels brutally physical. A solitary figure encounters an impossible swarm, loses control of the body piece by piece, and becomes host to something that treats flesh as raw material. Bones break. Insects burrow. The victim survives only in the technical sense, gradually becoming an alien deity whose transformation has erased whatever person existed before. The nastiest idea arrives afterward: worship. What begins as predation becomes conversion, and the ruined body becomes scripture. Consumption, reproduction, faith, and extermination collapse together until divinity itself starts looking like another parasitic infection. There is something wonderfully foul about that conception of godhood, especially coming from a band whose Southern gothic deathrock has long carried radical queer politics alongside its horror imagery. Authority here comes crawling out of meat. The slower passages give those images room to breathe before the faster sections shove everything toward panic. That contrast is crucial. Speed alone would turn the song into pursuit; the deliberate sections make you wait for whatever is chewing through the floorboards. By the final transformation, cosmic horror has lost every trace of abstraction. Infinity sprouts mandibles, theology breeds larvae, and salvation becomes a forced rebirth inside a body that has been converted into temple, nursery, and weapon. items.body: The screams of children, far away Echo in this perfect day A perfect society becomes considerably harder to admire once somebody explains who has been paying for it. In Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, an entire city’s happiness depends upon the suffering of a single child, an arrangement its citizens learn to accept as the price of their good fortune. There is plenty of room for horror in that cheerful consensus, especially once the people benefiting from it begin explaining why things simply have to be this way. Bologna’s La Mano Sinistra, whose name means “the left hand” in Italian, take up that ugly bargain on their debut single, Unnecessary Perfection. The track introduces Omelas, a seven-track concept album due November 6, 2026, through Bat-Cave Productions, translating Le Guin’s ethical dilemma into gothic rock with enough melodic momentum to carry its uncomfortable questions straight onto the dancefloor. A heartbeat rhythm opens the track, its alternating accents pressing against sustained, cold synthesizer tones before a thick, low-slung bassline sends everything forward. Guitar and electronics give the melody a generous sweep while Davide Sacco sings with the decadent authority of a frontman who can make a warning sound almost inviting. The combination brings to mind The Danse Society around their Heaven Is Waiting era, with something of Children on Stun and Brotherhood of Pagans in the vocal delivery and the way the instruments lock together. The guitar break ascends and descends through the melody, supplying an exhilarating lift while sustaining the chill of the surrounding synths. When Sacco’s voice returns alongside it, a more romantic quality enters his timbre, adding a strange tenderness to the accusation. This is the kind of gothic rock that makes getting dressed to go out feel like the opening scene of an evening full of possibilities. For a song about the moral cost of everybody having a good time, it has a wicked talent for getting the evening started. The lyrics initially survey a population blessed with sharp minds, untouched lives, and the promise of a cure for all, while concealed currents move beneath that reassuring surface. Sacco’s recurring question, “What’s necessary, what is not,” unsettles the supposed inevitability of the arrangement. By the closing lines, children’s screams carry across the distance into the perfect day itself. Read alongside Le Guin’s story, that distance becomes part of the accusation: comfort depends upon keeping suffering far enough away to be tolerated, even when its beneficiaries know exactly what sustains their happiness. The band describe the single this way: “The paradox of perfection. A fast-paced, impactful track reflecting the fictitious tranquility of a society built upon the distant screams of the weakest.” The accompanying video gives that selective vision an effective visual counterpart. High-contrast black-and-white performance footage is crossed by horizontal bands that repeatedly interrupt faces, instruments, and the lyrics appearing on screen. Close-ups of hands working the strings alternate with Sacco at the microphone, while the bars make even the plainest words momentarily difficult to see. The treatment suggests an uncomfortable connection between an obstructed image and a society accustomed to accepting a partial view. Watch the video for Unnecessary Perfection below: La Mano Sinistra brings together Sacco on vocals and lyrics, Gianluca Lo Presti of Nevica on bass and electronics, and Giuseppe Lo Bue of Caron Dimonio on guitar and electronics. Sacco is also a co-founder of the contemporary theatre company ErosAntEros and artistic director of POLIS Teatro Festival, a background that gives the project’s theatrical character a clear foundation. Omelas grew out of Sacco’s stage production of The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas, performed by actress Eva Robin’s. Recorded at Loto Studio in Ravenna during the summer of 2025, the album develops its source material across seven chapters, addressing indifference, collective guilt, and the decision to abandon a prosperity built upon injustice for an uncertain life beyond it. Unnecessary Perfection is available on digital platforms. Omelas follows on November 6, 2026, via Bat-Cave Productions. items.body: Rosetta Stone Executing Nostalgia Cleopatra Records Despite Porl King’s formal reactivation of the Rosetta Stone name happening a full seven years ago, it’s been remarkably tricky to pin down a specific sound or approach which has defined this era of King’s work. There have been reappraisals of interregnum work under the miserylab handle, syntheses of classic Rosetta Stone songwriting and modern production, and a suite of covers delivered with characteristic dryness which blurs the line between irony and earnestness. New release Executing Nostalgia embraces this amorphous fluidity, jamming all of King’s angles on goth rock into a dense forty minute listen. Without meaning to play armchair psychologist, I’d credit much of this restlessness to the question of King squaring the large bodies of work he recorded under the miserylab and Death It Ends from 2007 to 2018 with the idea of a “return” to Rosetta Stone. The legacy of In Death It Ends in particular may have been the key all along; from the moment a mesh of misty distorted guitar miasma joins the weighty, doomily reverbed bass and resigned, muttering vocals of opener “Shadowban”, that project’s unmistakable mix of classic darkwave and witchhouse is conjured up. There it remains for the remainder of the A-side of original material, mixed into spindly early Sisters fog machine goth on “Someone”, blended with miserylab minimalism on “Regression”, and compounded upon itself on the Soft Moon-like echoes of “Negative”. On the flip side, a set of five covers also sounds well-integrated and cooked down. Earlier tributes (“The Witch”, “Sisters Are Doing It For Themselves”) hinged upon deft yet tongue slightly in cheek elevations of naff source material to Rosetta Stone’s original, ornately stormy sound, but in choosing a set of ur-goth and relatedly dark tracks for Executing Nostalgia‘s back half, that issue vanishes. These are clearly tunes which helped shape King’s youthful tastes, and whether it’s the tempestuous “Incubus Succubus”, the high camp of the Prunes’ “Pagan Love Song”, or the sly shadowcraft of Colin Newman’s oft-overlooked “Alone”, they’re delivered forthrightly. From a purely musical perspective at this point in the Rosetta Stone reboot, opting to close the record with the looping, machine-like rhythmic punch of The Lorries’ “Talk About The Weather” is a subtle masterstroke. Partially made up of the sort of sparse clatter and jangle associated with miserylab but shot through with the sort of impassioned vocal vitriol which illuminated early Rosetta Stone material and the right winding guitar to suit, King’s version is almost slavishly true to the original, yet in that manner it draws together just about all the corners of his various epochs, a fitting marker of Rebooting Nostalgia‘s everything and the kitchen sink approach. items.body: New Jersey’s multifaceted world of underground music features a healthy amount of experimental jazz, mutating into various new and unique directions. In the same land that spawned Wayne Shorter, Sarah Vaughan and the famed Van Gelder studios, there seems to be an endless amount of artists pushing the boundaries on the genre today, from the hallucinatory prog-funk fusion of New Brunswick’s Guesstimate and Asbury Park’s We Used to Cut the Grass, to the improvisatory adventurousness of Paterson’s Thieves in Paris. Yet one name that always seems to appear while discussing the current state of Jersey jazz, and that is Mike Noordzy. From projects like El Noordzo, Mothguts and the Mike Noordzy Quintet, the Middlesex County-dwelling multi-instrumentalist never ceases to wow and amaze with his genre-defying sounds and unorthodox approaches. One of my favorite of his many albums was the shadowy avant-jazz soundscape that is Shark Funeral Songbook, released under his Noordzo moniker back in 2017. Nearly ten years later, he’s released a follow up, Shark Funeral Songbook Vol. 2, and it defied the odds and outshines the original. The album squirms and throbs with murky life, as it swings from percussion and string-based tracks that echo the works of Moondog, to surreal noir drifts and cataclysmic jazz-metal sludge and beyond. The album is a deep and varied collage of all kinds of styles and flavors, often blending and clashing together within a single track. The end result may offer hints of the likes of Tom Waits, Peter Brötzmann and, in the case of the harder tracks, Noordzy’s own Mothguts project, yet there is really no other album quite like this one. Between the collision of disparate genres, greasy textures, gritty atmospherics and unhinged rhythms all bleeding together within a very musique concrète-styled mix, this is a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience. The more you listen to this spooky record, the more you get pulled into its vastly immersive sonic world, and the more you feel like you’re getting a glimpse into the busy mind of a multifaceted artist who can channel their creativity into a thousand different directions at a moment’s notice. Boundless, unpredicatble and endlessly entertaining, Shark Funeral Songbook vol. 2 is a must have for fans of Sonny Sharrock, Colin Stetson and Moor Mother. items.body: What’s old is always new again. We got a full-blown nü metal revival on our hands, noise rock is arguably as popular as it’s ever been, and Myspace-era metalcore is getting about as many new releases from bands with members who were born around the same time the legends were laying the foundation. I was also recently reminded that fucking Greta Van Fleet exists for some godforsaken reason. For some other reason, I feel like we’ve just kinda skipped over a lot of good stuff. Where’s the grunge revival? Where’s the college-rock revival? Where’s the early post-punk revival? Where’s all the shit that sounds like it was made by people who hadn’t yet figured out what genre they were supposed to be in? Why does everyone nowadays sound so ready to be categorized?Well, Whippets make a case to step into these shoes, sounding something like Unwound by way of Dinosaur Jr. and Jay Reatard, or like Fugazi covering Dismemberment Plan and Siouxsie and the Banshees at the same time. They convey this volatile energy with writhing guitar leads that are often as eerie as they are anthemic, and tuneful bass in a rhythm section that paves the way for both their most unruly and airy moments. Much like their 2024 self-titled release, Whippets again flex their knack for melodies that get their hooks in your eardrums like velcro. No Skulls is every bit as fearless and without boundaries, gaining traction across a multitude of late 80s and early 90s soundscapes, regularly finding familiar touchpoints with the intuition to pull the rug at just the right time, or mix ‘n’ match influences in a way that’s as much “Aha!” as it is “What the fuck?” It’s like post-punk found the perfectly imperfect dancing partner in shoegaze, distraught while still finding an endearing footing, abrasive, oddly charming, and eyebrow-raising all at once.The video for album opener “These Woods” taps into a similar throwback, like it could’ve been dug out of a shoebox full of forgotten tapes and old zines. With a hazy camcorder look, sunbleached and spliced together with live footage, BMXers, scrapbook imagery, and other ’90s feels, it has the scrappy and surreal feel of something you might’ve stumbled across on MTV’s 120 Minutes at 1 a.m. It’s an appropriate visual companion, familiar enough to trigger a deeply buried memory, but weird enough to feel like you’ve never quite seen it before—and maybe even inspire a bad haircut.Check it out: No Skulls drops today, October 2, on wax and digital via No Coast Records.

items.body: Top PickTo The Grave – Liberation Front (brutal deathcore) To the Grave have been gradually refining their sound across their career, with previous outing Everyone's a Murderer (2024) being both their best and most uneven release yet. That album's development of a more traditional death metal sound made for some of their strongest single compositions to date, yet the album as a whole was hampered by a handful of misguided experiments that let a lot of fans, myself included, longing for more of the former and a lot less of the latter. Liberation Front does just that, continuing the band's enhanced trajectory by offering up 10 tracks of inhuman(e) brutality that each easily rank among their best and most belligerent. In that sense, it is probably To the Grave's most consistent record to date. At the same time though, there is a sameness to proceedings that makes the record somewhat less remarkable, and certainly less memorable, than each of their preceding releases. For all their vital volatility, this band seem to have a real problem with pacing and variation. Case in point is epic album-closing duology "Terrorfire" and "The World is a Slaughterhouse", the former of which is a moody manifesto and the later of which is perhaps the best and most ambitious of their compositions to date. They're the kind of tracks I'd love to see open a record and set the standard for what's to come, rather than being buried behind a wall of exhilarating yet highly exhausting preambles. The band themselves seem to be aware of this, having done almost exactly that when I caught them live last month, when they opened with "Terrorfire" into new track "Nail Mary". However, they still haven't worked out that they need to then drop the rabble rousing "DxE or Die" immediately afterwards to max out the momentum—instead frustratingly (and rather disappointingly) berating the crowd for being a bunch of "bitches" for a few more songs, rather than giving them a reason to really go off.Don't get me wrong, Liberation Front is still a monstrous record that accurately excused the outrage its subject matter ought to induce. It's just that, like pig-headed frontman Dane Evans himself exclaimed at that same show—and as the more digestible Still EP (2025) shows—"Holy shit, this is a lot of fucking brutal deathcore!" Like the common (mis)conception of the album's namesake, To the Grave continue to be a band defined more by their shortcomings than their successes, while still being one of the most exciting and ferocious modern deathcore bands in the game. Hopefully Liberation Front is simply an over-correction and the band will nail it next time, like a trio of grizzly bears gobbling down on a golden-locked intruder.Brymir – What We Leave Behind (progressive/symphonic viking-melodeath) Review The new Amon Amarth album is much better than their previous two, but still a long way off the run of seven or so records before that. Also... how much is the fish! 華やかな身振りで圧倒するのではなく、一音一音の行方を見つめ、沈黙まで音楽に変えてゆくピアニスト。17歳で第4位となった2015年大会から10年を経て、リーズ国際ピアノ・コンクール優勝などの実績を重ね、すでに国際的なキャリアを築いていた彼は、ワルシャワへ戻って、ついに頂点へ立った。 エリック・ルー（ピアノ） 1997年アメリカのマサチューセッツ州生まれ。ダン・タイ・ソンらに師事し、第19回ショパン国際ピアノ・コンクール（2025）で優勝。 2018年にはリーズ国際ピアノコンクールでも優勝した。思慮に富んだ、詩情あふれる力強い演奏により、すでに世界の音楽シーンでも際立ったアーティストの一人として定評を得ている。シカゴ響、ボストン響、ロンドン響、フィンランド放送響などのオーケストラや、ムーティ、ルイージ、ガードナー、ダウスゴーらの指揮者と共演し、アムステルダムのコンセルトヘボウ、ライプツィヒ・ゲヴァントハウス、シャンゼリゼ劇場などでリサイタルを行っている。ロンドンのウィグモアホールでは7年連続でリサイタルを開き、BBCプロムスやラ・ロック・ダンテロン音楽祭などにも出演。ワーナー・クラシックスと専属契約を結び、シューベルトのソナタ集や最新盤の即興曲集はBBCミュージック・マガジンの器楽部門推薦盤に選ばれるなど高い評価を得ており、国際的な賞も多数受賞している。 内省と熱狂をどう描くのか ～エリック・ルー ルーの美質は、繊細な音色と力強い高揚を矛盾なく両立させるところにある。 2025年のワルシャワの舞台でも、細やかな音色の陰影と、持続する緊張のなかに抑制された美を響かせる演奏が際立った。優勝後、ファビオ・ルイージ指揮・NHK交響楽団と共演したショパンの「ピアノ協奏曲 第2番」も、芯の通った美音と端正な構築を示す、いわば「渋い」秀演だった。 そうした内省的な表現が、ロシア・ロマン派を代表するチャイコフスキーの大協奏曲で、どこまで外へ開かれるのか。 耳なじみのある壮麗な和音で幕を開けるこの協奏曲だが、真価は豪快さだけにとどまらない。 有名な序奏の主題は二度と戻らず、音楽はウクライナ民謡に由来する主題へと進む。ピアノも常に主役でいるのではなく、ときに伴奏へ回り、木管と親密な言葉を交わし、やがて大管弦楽とともに巨大な頂点を築く。 ルーが内省と熱狂の振幅をどう描き、指揮者とオーケストラがその呼吸にどう応えるか。ここに今回の大きな聴きどころがある。コンクールで彼を知った人にとっても、新たな横顔に出会える公演となりそうだ。 ESOエバーグリーン交響楽団 × エリック・ルー 台湾から世界へ ～エバーグリーン・グループの理念の先へ 今回ルーが共演するのは、台湾のエバーグリーン交響楽団。 その名から、緑のロゴとラインが印象的なエバー航空の機体を思い浮かべる人もいるだろう。オーケストラと航空会社は同じエバーグリーン・グループに属し、エバーグリーン響は創業者・張栄発が設立した基金会のもと、2002年に発足した。 世界的にも珍しい、民間財団が運営するプロ・オーケストラであり、草創期から《雨夜花》《望春風》などの台湾民謡を管弦楽で演奏してきた。その響きは、エバー航空が台湾へ到着する際の機内音楽にも用いられてきた。 同社の便を利用した人なら、知らず知らずのうちにエバーグリーン響の演奏に触れているかもしれない。台湾に根差しながら世界へ向かうという理念を、まさに音で体現してきた楽団なのだ。 エバーグリーン交響楽団（ESO） 2002年、財団法人張栄発基金会によって設立されたエバーグリーン交響楽団（ESO）は、台湾で唯一の民間財団所属のプロフェッショナル・オーケストラである。「台湾に根差し、世界を志向する」という明確なビジョンのもと、優れた音楽人材の育成と、質の高いクラシック音楽の普及を使命としている。これまでにパヴァロッティ、ドミンゴ、カレラスの「世界三大テノール」をはじめ、アンドレア・ボチェッリ、ルネ・フレミング、ラン・ラン、チョーリャン・リン（林昭亮）など、世界的な巨匠たちと数多くの共演を重ねている。2025年1月からは世界的指揮者ヤープ・ヴァン・ズヴェーデンをアーティスト・イン・レジデンスに招聘し、2026年7月に東京・新潟公演を果たす。2026年以降もさらなる国際的展開を見据え、その活動の幅を広げ続けている。 筆者は今年3月、台北でエバーグリーン響のベートーヴェン《第九》を、7月には東京でマーラーの《子供の不思議な角笛》と交響曲第1番《巨人》を聴いた。 耳を捉えたのは、艶と厚みのある弦、各声部が明晰に噛み合う合奏力、そして、頂点へ向けてエネルギーを幾重にも積み上げる推進力だった。大編成が力を解放しても響きは鈍重にならず、音楽は筋肉質な輪郭を保って前進する。 一方、7月のマーラーでは、弦の上に独奏楽器が鮮やかに浮かび、精度の奥から、奏者たちの自発的な歌が聴こえてきた。 今年7月には東京と新潟でマーラーを聴かせたズヴェーデン＆エバーグリーン響 エバーグリーン響を「アジアの宝石」に ～ズヴェーデンの音楽づくり エバーグリーン響に変化をもたらしているのが、2025年からアーティスト・イン・レジデンスを務めるヤープ・ヴァン・ズヴェーデンである。 ロイヤル・コンセルトヘボウ管弦楽団のコンサートマスターから指揮者へ転じ、ダラス響、香港フィル、ニューヨーク・フィルを率いてきた。現在はソウル・フィルとフランス放送フィルの音楽監督を務めている。 ズヴェーデンの音楽づくりは精密で、ストイックだ。 速いテンポでも細部を曖昧にせず、リズムに強い芯を通し、声部の陰影を浮かび上がらせる。しかし、整然としているだけではなく、力強いグルーヴと、クライマックスへ向かって蓄積される熱を備えている。優れたヴァイオリン奏者としてオーケストラの内側を知る彼だけに、協奏曲でも独奏者を支えるだけでなく、ときに刺激し、ときにすっと引く立体的な対話が期待できる。 3月、台北で本人に取材した際、彼はエバーグリーン響を「アジアの宝石」に育てたいと語った。7月の東京・新潟公演からわずか3か月。今回の再来日公演は、その共同作業の現在地を確かめる絶好の機会である。 ヤープ・ヴァン・ズヴェーデン（指揮） 1960年アムステルダム生まれ。19歳でロイヤル・コンセルトヘボウ管弦楽団の史上最年少コンサートマスターに就任。1996年に指揮者へ転身し、オランダ放送フィルハーモニー管弦楽団首席指揮者（2005-2013／現在は名誉首席指揮者）、ダラス交響楽団音楽監督（2008-2018）、ニューヨーク・フィルハーモニック第26代音楽監督（2018-2024）を歴任した。現在、ニューヨーク・フィルハーモニックの音楽監督として2022年にデヴィッド・ゲフィン・ホールの歴史的な改修と再オープンを主導したほか、香港フィルハーモニー管弦楽団を国際的な地位へと押し上げ、ダラス交響楽団を全米屈指のアンサンブルへと成長させた。2024年からはソウル・フィルハーモニー管弦楽団の音楽監督に就任し、2025年からは台湾のエバーグリーン交響楽団のアーティスト・イン・レジデンス、そして2026年秋にはフランス放送フィルハーモニー管弦楽団の音楽監督への就任が決定している。オーケストラに対して明確な「ビジョンを聴き」、それを具現化する「マスター・ビルダー（名建築家）」と評される指揮者である。その卓越した芸術性は、彼が率いてきた数々の楽団を輝かしい成功へと導いてきた。 三者を味わうにふさわしい一夜 プログラムは、ラヴェル《ラ・ヴァルス》、チャイコフスキーのピアノ協奏曲、ショスタコーヴィチの交響曲第5番。この3曲は、エバーグリーン響とヴァン・ズヴェーデンの異なる表情を引き出す。 《ラ・ヴァルス》では、霧の中から姿を現す舞踏の色彩と、崩壊へ突き進む加速。チャイコフスキーでは、独奏者ルーとの緊密な対話。そして、ショスタコーヴィチでは、悲嘆、諧謔、行進、祈りがせめぎ合う巨大な構造を統御し、その多面性を描き分ける力が問われる。三者の持ち味を一夜でたっぷりと味わえる選曲だ。
